Gianni Infantino is facing a battle to stay afloat as Fifa president after his botched bid to sell off stakes in the World Cup to private investors resulted in a significant loss in support.

Italy has become the latest to officially pull their support for Infantino, joining England, Wales and other European nations have led the charge in withdrawing their endorsement of the Swiss-Italian for re-election in March 2027, while Uefa asserted that its boycott of Fifa competitions still stands in a bid to oust him from power.

The global players union, Fifpro, have also turned on Infantino, accusing him of a “profound abuse of presidential power” in an explosive statement.

However, Infantino’s allies have also surfaced, with the likes of Mexico and Argentina joining Caf, the African football governing body, in reaffirming support for the under-fire president.

As dominoes continue to fall, here is every country and confederation to have expressed their opposition or support for Infantino:

Who has withdrawn its support for Infantino?

Uefa 🇪🇺

Uefa, the governing body for Europe, has staunchly opposed Infantino’s leadership, insisting that its boycott of Fifa competitions still stands despite the sell-off scheme being scrapped.

It points to how there have not been “assurances” that attempts like the privatisation of the World Cup “to disfigure the game in this way will never be made again”.

The French Football Federation, however, have indicated to BBC Sport that they still intend to compete at next month’s U20 Women’s World Cup despite the confederation-wide boycott.

England 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿

The English FA are one of many European member associations to send a letter to Fifa withdrawing its support for Infantino’s re-election in 2027.

Infantino’s apology letter that was sent around on Wednesday night changed nothing for the FA, who was “deeply concerned about the lack of process and governance” surrounding his sell-off scheme.

open image in gallery FA chief executive Mark Bullingham (left) next to Gianni Infantino ( PA )

Wales 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁷󠁬󠁳󠁿

The Football Association of Wales were one of the first to send its letter withdrawing support for Infantino.

“The ‌recent failures in good governance, processes, ‌leadership, values, stakeholder management, communications and sound judgment ​have led us to a position ‌where Mr Infantino has lost the confidence of the FAW to ‌remain at the helm of world football,” a statement read. “Failing to put the best interests of football first is a failure we cannot accept.”

Scotland 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁳󠁣󠁴󠁿

The SFA’s chief executive Ian Maxwell told the BBC that the governing body’s position has “been clear” since Uefa’s collective statement.

“We have aligned ourselves with the Uefa position and 55 nations are stronger than one voice.

“Their statement since then has talked about a lack of confidence in the Fifa leadership and the Scottish FA agree completely with that decision.

“The SFA will not be voting for Gianni Infantino come the re-election in early 2027.”

Republic of Ireland 🇮🇪

The Football Association of Ireland (FAI) has followed in withdrawing its support for Infantino while backing Uefa’s stance.

"Following an FAI board meeting, the decision was taken to rescind the letter of support that the Association supplied earlier this year," it confirmed. "It has since written to Fifa to explain its reasoning. The Association is grateful for the support that Fifa provides to Irish football, but recent events have raised significant concerns regarding governance, transparency and the lack of meaningful consultation.”

Italy 🇮🇹

The Italian Football Federation (FIGC) took a few weeks to take official action but it has now withdrawn its support for Infantino's candidacy in the next Fifa presidential election scheduled.

"This decision is intended to clearly and transparently express the FIGC's position - in full agreement with Uefa and its president Aleksander Ceferin - regarding the recent initiatives promoted by the FIFA president concerning the governance and development of international competitions," FIGC said in a statement.

Finland 🇫🇮

Finland kickstarted this process, with it being revealed that the Scandinavian member association was the first to send a letter officially withdrawing support for Infantino.

Serbia 🇷🇸

The Football Association of Serbia then sent a similar letter to Fifa.

“We would like to remind you that we provided our support to Mr Infantino in writing on 25 May of this year, but after carefully considering the events that have seriously damaged the image and reputation of both Fifa and its president in the past period, this is the only logical and rational course of action,” a statement read.

Sweden 🇸🇪

Sweden’s federation (SvFF) followed suit: "At an extraordinary board meeting on Monday, SvFF has chosen not to support Fifa President Gianni Infantino ​in the upcoming re-election.

"This is after a long-term assessment of the development within Fifa and the organization's leadership. The decision is based on recurring shortcomings in governance, transparency and management, which means that trust in Gianni Infantino's leadership no longer exists."

open image in gallery Infantino has officially lost the endorsement of numerous Uefa nations ( PA )

Croatia 🇭🇷

As did the Croatian Football Federation (HNS): "The Croatian Football Federation has informed Fifa of its decision to withdraw the support previously expressed for Mr Gianni Infantino's candidature for another term as Fifa president.

"This decision followed a thorough reassessment within the federation in light of recent developments surrounding the Fifa World Cup 2026 and discussions within our governing bodies. We consider our position to be clearly communicated to Fifa and have no further comment to add at this time."

Albania 🇦🇱

The Albanian Football Federation also took the same stance, aligning with Uefa.

“The Albanian Football Association has sent an official letter to Fifa Secretary General Mattias Grafström, informing him that it has withdrawn its support for Mr Gianni Infantino’s candidacy for another four-year term as Fifa President,” the statement confirmed.

Greece 🇬🇷

The Greek federation similarly sent their withdrawal of support Fifa’s way.

New Zealand 🇳🇿

New Zealand have broken rank with Oceania’s confederation by withdrawing their support for Infantino.

"After careful consideration, NZF has formed the view that decisions and actions within Fifa have contributed to a breakdown in trust and increased division within international football, and that an independent review is required to restore confidence and trust,” a statement read.

Who is also opposing Infantino?

Concacaf (Confederation for North America and the Caribbean) 🌎

Concacaf have come out in opposition of Infantino after being left stunned at the lack of consultation during the Fifa sell-off plan, which they went on to reject.

After the plan was aborted, the confederation said: “This recent unilateral and egregious act of poor governance and leadership follows a pattern of missteps and similar behaviour. A comprehensive reckoning with this presidency is imperative.”

It also wrote a joint statement with Uefa and the AFC which intended to give Infantino the opportunity to resign with dignity.

Concacaf president Victor Montagliani is widely being seen as a front-runner to challenge Infantino in next March’s election.

open image in gallery Concacaf president Victor Montagliani is widely being seen as a front-runner to challenge Infantino ( Getty )

AFC (Asian Football Confederation) 🌏

The AFC was similarly aggrieved by the non-existent consultation from Fifa regarding the Infantino’s scheme, rejecting the proposal before calling on Fifa to undertake an “urgent review of its governance”.

The confederation’s part in a joint statement with Uefa and Concacaf confirms their desire to see Infantino ousted from power.

Germany 🇩🇪

The German federation (DFB) already opted against endorsing Infantino earlier in the year so has not had to send a letter withdrawing support to take an opposing stance.

“The DFB has not signed a letter of support for the re-election of Gianni Infantino," the governing body stated in July. "Further steps will be discussed in the DFB presidential board."

Denmark 🇩🇰

Denmark are in a similar position to Germany, having not endorsed Infantino’s re-election bid prior to the scheme’s reveal.

There is also a precedent for their opposition to Infantino, with federation president Jesper Moller not supporting his re-election efforts back in 2022: “There is only one candidate ... but Denmark will not be supporting the current president.”

Norway 🇳🇴

The Norwegian Football Federation (NFF) have been one of the most vocal bodies to call for Infantino’s resignation, and while they have not yet officially sent a letter to withdraw their support in him, such action is expected in the coming days.

NFF president Lise Klaveness told the Guardian: “We decided that there is no trust in Infantino now. We have been worried consistently and there has been one more step in worrying direction every year, every part of the year. The trust is now gone for us, there is no way back for Infantino.

“We’re left in a very polarised cooperation globally and, I would say, chaos. So we will ask him to resign immediately so that the global football community can look ahead and cooperate going into the future.”

open image in gallery Lise Klaveness has called on Infantino to resign ( Reuters )

Netherlands 🇳🇱

The Royal Dutch Football Association (KNVB) is also yet to officially withdraw its support but is among the many to have confirmed it has lost confidence in Infantino’s leadership.

“The way this process has unfolded has resulted in a fundamental loss of confidence in the leadership of Fifa President Gianni Infantino. The KNVB no longer has confidence in his leadership,” a statement read.

Romania 🇷🇴

The Romanian Football Federation (FRF) were among the countries to resolutely reject the sell-off proposal, calling it “a dangerous initiative to turn football into a private asset.

As a result, the FRF will withold support for Infantino’s re-election for the time being, with a statement reading: “FRF is suspending the discussion regarding the support of Fifa President Gianni Infantino for a new term, until further clarifications.”

Northern Ireland ☘️

The Northern Irish football association (IFA) has expressed “concerns” over Infantino’s leadership but has not officially withdrawn its support yet, unlike neighbours Ireland.

"We take our responsibilities as a member association of both Uefa and Fifa seriously," said an IFA spokesperson. "We support the current Uefa position on the matter and will continue to engage constructively on issues relating to football governance. We are of course aware of the recent developments and wider concerns within the football community. We are considering these matters carefully and will continue to engage through the appropriate governance structures and channels.”

Jordan 🇯🇴

Jordan are so far the only non-Uefa member association to publicly oppose Infantino after federation president Prince Ali bin Hussein levelled accusations of blackmail against Fifa.

Prince Ali alleged the organisation offered assistance with the kingdom's issues in exchange for his endorsement, following Infantino's withdrawal from a World Cup stake sale proposal. Among the problems cited was the association's eight-month wait for prize money, due since December for reaching the Arab Cup final in Qatar.

After taking to X to reveal the outstanding payments, the Jordan Football Association received the prize money two days later - but Prince Ali has not changed his stance over not endorsing Infantino: “It does not change my clear position concerning the leadership of Fifa: my FA and I will not endorse president Infantino, nor will we vote for him.”

Sierra Leone 🇸🇱

Former Sierra Leone FA president and ex-Fifa Council member Isha Johansen has indicated that Africa’s support of Infantino is not unanimous across the continent after emerging as one of the African voices opposing the privatisation project.

He urged African football chiefs to think carefully about the game’s future, saying: "What price does one have to pay in order to get to this elevated development for football in Africa?"

Canada 🇨🇦

Canada prime minister Mark Carney joined his UK counterpart Andy Burnham in calling for Infantino to be ousted from his position as president.

“It should be fatal,” Carney said, whose country co-hosted this summer’s World Cup. “Certainly I don’t have confidence in Mr Infantino."

However, the country has confirmed it will not boycott Fifa competitions and participate in the U20 Women’s World Cup in Poland.

Guyana 🇬🇾

The Guyanese Football Federation, a South American nation under Concacaf but surrounded by Conmebol’s Infantino allies, has “fully endorsed” Concacaf’s statement condemning Infantino’s leadership.

“Good governance, transparency, accountability and institutional integrity remain fundamental principles that guide the work of the Guyanese Football Federation,” a statement read.

Recommended The Curacao blueprint and how Guyana are targeting a similar World Cup miracle

Who is supporting Infantino?

Caf (African Football Confederation) 🌍

Caf, the governing body for African football, has become the first confederation to unanimously back Infantino. Its 54 member associations account more than a quarter of Fifa’s 211 members.

“We are committed to continue working together with Fifa, its member associations, other football confederations and stakeholders to safeguard and adhere to governance, due process, and transparency global best practises and to contribute to the development and growth of football worldwide,” Caf president Patrice Motsepe said.

Motsepe later added thar the position of embattled president Infantino can only be decided by Fifa elections.

Conmebol (Confederation for South America) 🌎

Conmebol, the governing body for South America, expressed “concern about the repeated unilateral actions taken” and welcomed the decision to withdraw the plans, affirming it will “not support any action” that “ignores or deviates” from the “democratic procedures that represent the 211 Fifa member associations”.

However, as a long-time ally of Infantino, it has endorsed him to get elected for a third term, with Conmebol eager for his 64-team World Cup plans to go through for the 2030 edition.

Argentina 🇦🇷

Argentina became the first member from South America to voice its support for Infantino, on the same day that confederation Conmebol - which had thus far only expressed support of Infantino - expressed concern over Fifa’s procedures.

"Of our highest consideration, on behalf of the Argentine Football Association (AFA), and its Executive Committee, we address you, dear President, and through your worthy intermediary the Fifa board, to express our support for the management carried out during the last 10 years, which had as its main axes the development of football throughout the world and institutional solidity based on a clear governance model, stable and transparent,” a statement read.

open image in gallery Argentina president Javier Milei (left) behind Infantino at the "Board of Peace" hosted by US president Donald Trump ( AFP/Getty )

Mexico 🇲🇽

Mexico joined Argentina from the Americas, breaking rank from the United States, Canada and the rest of Concacaf that had condemned Infantino’s plan and aligned itself against his leadership.

The Mexican Football Federation (FMF) stated: "The FMF will neither recognise nor approve any process convened outside of that institutional framework, and it joins the call made... by President Infantino to collectively continue developing football for the benefit of the 211 member associations."

Grenada 🇬🇩

Grenada’s federation (GFA) has also broken away from the Concacaf block and reaffirmed its support for Infantino.

“The GFA reaffirms its support for Fifa President Gianni Infantino and expresses its sincere appreciation for his continued support for football development in Grenada and across the Caribbean over his period of service in office and for the years to come,” a statement read.

Saint Kitts and Nevis 🇰🇳

Like Grenada, the Saint Kitts and Nevis Football Association (SKNFA) has welcomed Infantino’s decision to scrap the plan, called for respect of Fifa’s institutional processes and backed the president to continue.

It said: “The SKNFA concluded by reaffirming its support for Infantino’s leadership and vision, and said it looks forward to supporting him as he completes his current constitutional mandate and continues efforts to advance football development across Fifa’s 211 Member Associations.”

Paraguay 🇵🇾

Paraguay has also followed suit as Infantino’s Conmebol support base begins to surface.

Their federation published a letter of support addressed to Infantino, writing that it "reaffirms its commitment to continue working alongside Fifa”.

Qatar 🇶🇦

Qatar was the first football association to publicly back Infantino, even though they later welcomed the decision to scrap the plan.

"While the proposal had merit, we applaud the wisdom behind prioritising unity among member associations. The Qatar Football Association fully supports President Infantino's efforts to continue growing and strengthening the game globally,” a statement read.

open image in gallery Qatar's FA has backed Infantino to continue as president ( Getty Images )

Sri Lanka 🇱🇰

Like Qatar, Sri Lanka welcomed the decision to scrap the investment plan and has since reaffirmed its support for Infantino.

"One of President Infantino's defining leadership qualities has always been his willingness to listen to the views and concerns of Member Associations. This decision is a clear reflection of his inclusive leadership style, built on dialogue, mutual respect, and a genuine commitment to serving the global football community," its statement read.

Kuwait 🇰🇼

Like others, Kuwait welcomed the decision to halt the plans but Sheikh Ahmed Yusuf Al-Sabah, the president of the Kuwait Football Association, affirmed his support for Infantino.

A statement read: “He concluded by affirming the Kuwait Football Association's confidence in the leadership of Fifa President Gianni Infantino, and its support for efforts aimed at developing the game and enhancing its opportunities for growth in a way that serves all national associations and achieves the shared interests of global football.”

Lebanon 🇱🇧

Lebanon, who granted Infantino citizenship last year, have backed the Swiss-Italian, with FA president Hashim Haidar all but echoing the same sentiments as Kuwait.

“Haidar reaffirms the Lebanese Football Association’s support for Fifa President Gianni Infantino and his confidence in the decisions he makes in the best interests of global football, as well as in his efforts and initiatives aimed at developing the game,” he said, while also asserting that Infantino’s proposal “could be re-examined ... in a away that serves the greater good of the sport and preserves its unity”.

Indonesia 🇮🇩

The president of the Indonesian FA supported Infantino’s sell-off plan and has now backed him for another term.

Hailing Fifa as a “strategic partner that is truly present” in its football development, Erick Thohir said: “This is proof of President Infantino’s vision that football development must not be centered on a single region; it must proceed worldwide.”

Philippines 🇵🇭

Philippines have also backed Infantino and backed for co-operation among confederations.

"We stand behind President Gianni Infantino's leadership, and trust that continued dialogue among all confederations and member associations will keep the global game moving forward together,” the Philippines confirmed.

Mongolia 🇲🇳

Joining the Philippines, the Mongolian Football Federation has put out a statement in support of Infantino.

Bhutan 🇧🇹

The Bhutan Football Federation has published a letter that extends its “sincere appreciation” to Infantino for scrapping the plans, hailing him for demonstrating “true leadership” by “prioritising consensus over commerce”.

“We stand united with Fifa and President Infantino in their ongoing efforts to serve the global football community,” wrote federation president Dasho Ugen Tsechup.

Morocco 🇲🇦

The location of Infantino’s crisis meeting on Wednesday, Morocco have stuck by the Swiss-Italian as one of his most loyal allies.

“What has been achieved in recent years through Fifa’s development programmes, particularly in Africa, represents an important accomplishment that must be preserved, to the benefit of all member associations,” said the Royal Moroccan Football Federation’s president Fouzi Lekjaa.

open image in gallery Infantino held his crisis meeting in Rabat, Morocco ( AP )

Egypt 🇪🇬

Similar to their north African counterpart, Egypt have maintained their endorsement of Infantino.

"The Egyptian Football Association reiterates its full trust in President Gianni Infantino's leadership and its continuous support for any initiatives that benefit Fifa member associations and the future of world football,” a statement read.

Mauritania 🇲🇷

Ahmed Yahya, the country's representative on the Fifa Council, was one of a number of African football leaders to say he was backing Infantino early on, pledging his support before Caf took its stance.

Niger 🇳🇪

Same as above, with Hamidou Djibrilla from Niger coming out quickly in support of Infantino.

Sudan 🇸🇩

Sudan’s federation joined five other Arab nations - Qatar, Lebanon, Morocco, Egypt and Mauritania - in writing a joint statement backing Infantino.

"Recognising the important role of Arab football in bringing people together and strengthening co-operation among football associations across the Arab world, we ... express our full support for Mr Gianni Infantino, president of Fifa, and reaffirm our confidence in his leadership and continued commitment to the development of football worldwide," the statement read.

"We deeply appreciate Mr Infantino’s sustained efforts to advance football globally, expand opportunities across all regions and strengthen the game’s role in bringing people and communities together. We look forward to continuing our close cooperation with him towards a stronger and more prosperous future for world ‌football, expanding opportunities and further enhancing Arab football’s contribution to ​the global game."

DR Congo 🇨🇩

DR Congo's federation (Fecofa) president Veron Mosengo-Omba, who was only elected in May, spoke out in “full support”. of Infantino. The two studied at university in Switzerland together.

Fecofa said it had "greatly benefited" from Fifa's programmes, citing investment in development and infrastructure.

Nigeria 🇳🇬

The Nigeria Football Federation (NFF) has largely aligned itself towards a supportive stance for Infantino's leadership, with former NFF president and deputy chairman of Fifa's Men's National Teams Competitions Committee, Amaju Pinnick, backing his initial sell-off plan.

Comoros 🇰🇲

The president of the Comoros Football Federation, Said Ali Athouman, also backed Infantino’s scheme due to the financial benefits to smaller nations.

"Our problem is how to obtain money,” he said. “Right now, we have no sponsors. So how do we compete? The richest nations can train players, have infrastructure and equipment, and it's no coincidence that they then achieve results. Most European countries don't have ​these problems.”

open image in gallery A number of African nations have fallen in line with the stance of Caf president Patrice Motsepe ( Getty )

Malawi 🇲🇼

Fleetwood Haiya, Malawi's football chief, echoed the same concerns in his support for Infantino.

He told BBC Sport: "Our government is not able to make sure that they have medical supplies in hospitals and at the same time to look at football. Malawi needs money."

Uganda 🇺🇬

The Ugandan federation are said to have echoed Malawi’s sentiments, with football officials from the federation telling BBC Sport that Fifa investment has transformed their game both on and off the pitch.

Gambia 🇬🇲

Lamin Kaba Bajo told BBC Sport that his federation not just stood by Infantino, but would do "everything within our means" to get him re-elected.

"That's my personal opinion as president of the federation, and a good number of African memberships also stand on that line. He is here to stay,” he said.

Djibouti 🇩🇯

The Djiboutian Football Federation has similarly welcomed the decision to withdraw the sell-off proposal, with president Souleiman Hassan Waberi saying the climbdown “demonstrates a firm commitment to preserving the unity, solidarity and cohesion that define the football family”.

He said in a statement: “I reaffirm my full support for Fifa President Mr Gianni Infantino and for all initiatives aimed at promoting the sustainable, transparent and inclusive development of football around the world.”

South Africa 🇿🇦

While not an official statement from the federation, South Africa’s Minister of Sports, Arts and Culture of South Africa, Gayton McKenzie, posted on X saying that Infantino had been "very good to African football".

"Africa should be cautious in joining the public lynching of Infantino,” he warned. “He has been very good to African football. We can debate his ideas but let's not forget who has been a friend to us. Many of those calling for his head want the old status quo back too."

Who is yet to take a stance?

The Oceania Football Confederation (OFC) stopped short from pulling its support for Infantino in their statement after welcoming the scrapping of the sell-off plan, very much staying on the fence as it called for a “review”.

A statement read: "The OFC recognises the progress achieved over the last decade in advancing football development in Oceania under Fifa's leadership and encourages Fifa to use the review as an opportunity to identify and implement any changes that may be necessary."

Meta will pay up to $17.1 billion and make sweeping changes to Instagram and Facebook to settle a major US court case.

The company has been fighting a lawsuit against the attorneys general of 29 US states, who accused it of knowingly damaging young people’s wellbeing with its platforms.

Now, the two sides have reached a settlement that commits Meta to bring in a host of changes, including daily limits and nighttime blocks on teenagers’ accounts on Instagram and Facebook. Young people will also be blocked from being able to see the number of likes or reactions to posts.

In advance of the case, it had been hailed as a major opportunity for Meta and its chief executive Mark Zuckerberg to answer claims that it had harmed children. The hearings had already brought a series of dramatic accusations, including claims that Meta had deliberately hidden evidence of the ways that its platforms were damaging young people’s mental health.

But, overnight, reports suggested that Meta and states attorneys general were working towards a mid-trial settlement that would bring the hearings to an end. Meta, which has always denied the claims in the case, did not admit to wrongdoing as part of the newly announced settlement.

The major case is just one part of a range of legal actions and regulatory investigations into Meta. States, local governments, school districts and individuals have alleged that ⁠Meta and other social media companies fueled a nationwide youth mental health crisis.

Those behind the case hailed the settlement as a major success – and suggested that more, similar actions are likely to come in the future. They hailed it as the largest settlement against Big Tech ever, and the biggest consumer protections agreement of its kind in history outside of the Big Tobacco settlements of the 1990s.

“Meta intentionally exploited kids for profit and then lied about it, claiming its products were safe when its own internal research confirmed the platforms were addictive and harmful,” said Brian L Schwalb, attorney general for the District of Columbia. “This is a monumental public health victory for young people in DC and across the country, and the safety features Meta is required to install will fundamentally and immediately change how young people use Instagram and Facebook.

“The physical, mental, and emotional harms that intentionally addictive social media platforms inflict on youth — and particularly teenage girls — are widespread across the tech industry, and this successful, coordinated multistate litigation has resulted in Meta being the first platform to come to the table and agree to such comprehensive reforms. It will not be the last.”

The settlement requires Meta to pay at least $12.1 billion to resolve the lawsuits, over a period of ten years. That could increase by another $5 billion, depending on agreements with other major social media companies.

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg attends a dinner hosted by US President Donald Trump with tech leaders for a dinner in the State Dining Room of the White House in Washington, DC, on September 4, 2025. (Photo by SAUL LOEB / AFP) (Photo by SAUL LOEB/AFP via Getty Images) ( AFP/Getty )

It also forces Meta to bring in a host of changes to its platforms, aimed at protecting the young people who use them. They include a host of restrictions on when and how the sites can be used, as well as blocks on certain features and new tools to allow parents to help ensure their children’s safety.

Instagram and Facebook will limit children’s use of Instagram and Facebook together to two hours a day, with pauses every 15 minutes to interrupt people who are continuously scrolling. Those limits will last for five years, but will drop to 60 minutes for 10 years if Snapchat, TikTok and YouTube adopt similar rules.

Children will also be blocked from accessing the sites overnight. They will be banned between midnight and 6am, and notifications will be silenced between 10pm and 7am.

Children will also be limited in their access to the apps through the school day. The services will not be able to send push notifications to children between 8am and 3pm during the school year.

The company must also introduce better checks to verify the age of young users, and increased content controls to ensure that young people are protected from content about bullying, eating disorders, and suicide and self-harm. Meta must also introduce stronger and more user-friendly parental controls as well as limiting access to features such as beauty filters and “like” counts that encourage unhealthy social comparison between young people.

Meta’s implementation of those features will be regularly checked by an independent auditor to ensure they are working, the settlement says. That process will be overseen by the states that have reached the settlement.

News.title: Meteorologist bursts into uncontrollable giggles during live broadcast
News.content:
A weather presenter burst into uncontrollable laughter during a live report on Sunday (23 August).

A fit of giggles overcame WABI-TV meteorologist Patrick Osborn, who later revealed that the outburst was due to a prank that "kind of backfired."

Osborn had to step off screen as he could not stop laughing, asking a colleague to take over.

He later explained that he had been trying to prank anchor Josh Gabbard by playing a Charlie Brown "wa wa wa" sound during a commercial break, but the clip was longer than they expected and played during his segment, which set Osborn's giggles off.

The draw for the Carabao Cup third round takes place this evening as more teams from the Premier League, including holders Manchester City, enter the competition and learn who they will face.

Most top-flight clubs, such as Chelsea and Tottenham, entered the tournament in the second round with those who are competing in European competitions this season now involved as well. Arsenal, Liverpool and Manchester United are also among those to enter at this stage.

Their participation also means that the third round will be played across two midweeks in order for the teams involved in the Champions League, Europa League and Conference League to juggle their match schedules.

Here’s everything you need to know about the draw

When is the Carabao Cup third round draw?

The draw for the Carabao Cup third round will take place today, Wednesday 26 August. The main draw will follow the conclusion of the second round tie between Preston and Everton which kicks off at 8pm BST, meaning the draw could start at around 10.15pm BST.

How will the draw work?

Pre-draw

Before the main draw, there is a pre-draw to decide if the eight Champions League and Europa League clubs will be at home or away. This part is before Preston North End’s Round Two tie against Everton on Sky Sports.

Main draw

The main draw will take place following the conclusion of Round Two tie, the first eight ties will involve those Champions League and Europa League clubs. Their home or away position will have already having been decided. They will then be drawn against a team in a separate bowl with the remaining teams in the competition – so cannot meet one another at this stage.

Following the conclusion of those eight ties being drawn, the final eight ties will be drawn as normal.

From Round Three onwards, there is no longer a divide between the Northern and Southern sections.

How can I watch the Carabao Cup draw?

The Carabao Cup third-round draw will be shown live on Sky Sports Main Event and Sky Sports Football following the conclusion of Preston v Everton.

Sky Sports subscribers will also be able to watch the draw live online via the Sky Go app.

Which teams are involved?

32 teams are involved in the draw including 23 winners of second round ties and nine additional Premier League clubs who are also competing in European competitions this season.

Those teams in Europe and entering the competition for the first time this season are: Arsenal, Aston Villa, Bournemouth, Brighton & Hove Albion, Crystal Palace, Liverpool, Manchester City, Manchester United and Sunderland.

Of those, Brighton can be in Europe through the Conference League, but that competition does not begin until October, so it does not affect the Round Three schedule.

The third round of the Carabao Cup is scheduled to take place across consecutive weeks, starting on 7 September and 14 September. The ties will be played midweek as single-leg fixtures with the winners progressing to the fourth round.

President Donald Trump’s personal assistant Natalie Harp enjoyed a special perk when she first joined his team that raised eyebrows among fellow staffers, according to author Michael Wolff.

Harp, 35, a former One America News anchor, has become a fixture at Trump’s side since 2022 and has recently attracted attention over the nature of their relationship after Wolff obtained a pair of gushing letters in which she expressed her devotion to him, writing: “You are all that matters to me.”

Speaking to The Daily Beast’s Inside Trump’s Head podcast, Wolff – the author of several controversial books about the president, including Fire and Fury (2018) and All or Nothing (2025) – revealed that Harp’s being granted access to an exclusive, all-you-can-eat Sunday buffet at Trump’s golf club in West Palm Beach, Florida, was met with astonishment by her fellow employees.

“The staffers... like, I mean, they get teary-eyed, their eyes roll back, because they’re actually not allowed to go to the buffet,” Wolff told the show’s co-host Joanna Coles Tuesday, emphasizing its bountiful, “over the top” spread, offering ham, lobster, omelettes and fresh fruit.

“Natalie was always allowed into the buffet,” he continued. “Not just Natalie, but Natalie with her mother. Among the staff there was like, ‘Is she allowed to do that? Should she be doing that?’

open image in gallery Michael Wolff discusses President Donald Trump's personal assistant Natalie Harp on the Inside Trump's Head podcast ( Inside Trump's Head/The Daily Beast )

“And then the people at the golf club serving this: ‘Should we?... She says that the president says she can be here, but can she be here?’ That became... a major moment within the campaign: Natalie at the buffet.”

Wolff told the same podcast last week that concerned staffers had tipped him off about Harp’s letters to the president.

“They were worried that this person, Natalie Harp, who was then 30 years old... no background whatsoever, had come to... take more and more and more of... candidate Trump’s attention, and become more and more central to what he knew, what he believed, the opinions that he had at any given moment,” he said.

Prior to their publication, Harp had already provoked media interest after it emerged she was one of the select members of the president’s entourage he had chosen to join him in being whisked away from a Turkish airport in July in a secret secondary plane – which he had boarded via a catering truck – after Iran made a threat against his life.

While the likes of Secretary of State Marco Rubio, White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt and the traveling press corps were left aboard Air Force One, Trump, Harp and fellow aides Dan Scavino and Walt Nauta escaped to the U.K. together before rejoining their colleagues to cross the Atlantic.

open image in gallery Harp has attracted close media scrutiny in recent weeks over the nature of her relationship with the president after a pair of gushing letters she sent him were published ( AFP/Getty )

After the emergence of the letters, in which she also told Trump she felt “unworthy” of serving him, MS NOW reported that Harp had gone more than a year without securing the routine security clearance West Wing staffers are usually expected to obtain, raising concerns about what classified material she might have seen.

White House spokesman Davis Ingle has told The Independent that Harp “is one of the most loyal and hardest-working aides on President Trump’s team.”

He has also attacked the journalist at the center of the storm, saying in a statement: “Michael Wolff is a professional scumbag and serial liar whose brain has been completely warped by his severe and incurable disease known as Trump Derangement Syndrome.”

The focus on Harp has nevertheless been used as a stick with which to beat the president.

Georgia Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff said at a rally in Atlanta last week: “He doesn’t want to do his job. He wants to build his ballroom and travel with Natalie on their apparently defenseless flying palace gifted by the Emir of Qatar.”

open image in gallery Harp is rarely far from Trump’s side and has become the subject of mockery from Democrats ( Getty )

Leavitt, Ingle and White House Communications Director Steven Cheung all attacked Ossoff, as did CNN’s resident conservative Scott Jennings, demanding that he apologize for the insinuating remark, but he has so far declined to do so.

Trump himself angrily compared the senator to the 1980s children’s entertainer Pee-Wee Herman, leading Ossoff to stand back and admire the “meltdown” he had inspired.

Michigan Democratic Rep. Debbie Dingell has since followed suit, responding to Trump’s threat to rename Lake Ontario amid his trade feud with Canada by suggesting rechristening it “Lake Natalie” in Harp’s honor.

News.title: Livestock bacterial disease spreading among humans in Europe
News.content:
In Barcelona, researchers found further evidence that the bacterium was spreading between people.

Nine cases identified between December 2025 and March 2026 were caused by strains that differed by just zero to four genetic mutations, suggesting the infections were part of a recent transmission chain rather than separate cases acquired from animals.

The bacterium can survive in crusted areas on the skin for up to 42 months, according to Dr McHale, raising questions about the role of contaminated surfaces, equipment and shared spaces.

People should not be alarmed by the infection, which is treatable with a course of antibiotics, he added.

This could make hygiene particularly important in places such as saunas, where people may have prolonged skin contact with others and with shared surfaces.

Saunas have historically been a destination for gay and bisexual men seeking social and sexual contact.

Dating apps such as Grindr have since made casual encounters in these environments far easier to arrange, experts say.

“What we’re seeing is the kind of in-person venues like saunas being combined with apps,” said Rusi Jaspal, a Professor of Psychology at the University of Brighton and expert on wellbeing among gay men.

“Someone might, for example, be in a sauna but also have their app on, and that might be a way of getting people to come to the sauna. So they’re not only attracting people who are already in the sauna, but who might be outside of that environment and coming in.”

Progress and complacency

Professor Jaspal believes the success of Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP), which protects against HIV, has also played a role.

“I think that is a really big contributor,” he said. “On the one hand, obviously it’s fantastic that PrEP is there. It prevents HIV; it’s extremely effective against HIV. But it’s not effective against other infections.”

He argued that because PrEP has removed the fear of HIV that shaped gay men’s sexual behaviour for decades, some men are now having condomless sex with more partners, in the belief that other infections are treatable in a way HIV once was not.

“Because they think, well, everything else is treatable – gonorrhoea, syphilis, it’s all treatable – they’re going to just not use condoms,” he said. “That is not only creating more of a risk of infection, but I think people are having more partners as well.”

Sexual contact is not the only route by which the bacterium appears to be spreading.

In Norway, ten cases have been linked to martial arts, with some infections occurring during training in Norway and others during trips to Thailand.

One case report described a 34-year-old Muay Thai fighter who developed recurrent pustular lesions after returning from a training trip, later confirmed as D. congolensis through whole-genome sequencing.

Dr McHale said the bacterium tends to take hold where the skin has already been compromised in some way.

“Predisposing factors for infection include cutaneous microtrauma, for example, from ultraviolet radiation, tick exposure and insect bites, and maceration of the skin,” he said.

Dermatophilus congolensis is notoriously difficult to grow in culture, meaning infections can easily go undiagnosed or be mistaken for more common skin conditions.

Researchers in Barcelona have warned that cases could be going unrecognised because sexual health clinics do not routinely test for the bacterium.

But Professor Jaspal believes the legacy of the HIV/Aids epidemic explains why this cluster was identified so quickly.

He said the crisis of the 1980s, when confusion and stigma allowed the virus to spread largely undetected, forced public health bodies to build far stronger surveillance and communication systems for outbreaks among gay and bisexual men.

That same infrastructure, he argued, has since been used to manage subsequent threats such as mpox – and now this obscure bacterium – far more effectively.

“I think we are quite rightly identifying cases early on, so that we can then communicate that risk to people and encourage precautions to protect themselves,” Professor Jaspal said. “That is really, really important.”

News.title: The five best coastal places to retire in the UK
News.content:
How equity release can help you purchase a seaside property

UK homeowners aged 55 or over may be able to use equity release in two main ways: either to help fund the purchase of a second home, or to buy a new home and release equity from that property as part of the same legal transaction. Seeking professional advice is key to understanding which option may be right for you.



The most popular equity release product is a lifetime mortgage. A lifetime mortgage is a loan secured against your home. It will reduce the value of your estate and could affect your entitlement to means-tested benefits. There is no obligation to make monthly repayments with a lifetime mortgage, although you can choose to make some if you wish. Instead, the full amount plus interest is only repaid when the last homeowner dies or enters permanent long-term care, and this is usually done with the sale of the home.



You must always seek professional help when considering equity release. Make sure your adviser is looking at products from lenders that are members of the Equity Release Council. The Equity Release Council, the industry trade body, requires its members to offer plans that comply with its product standards.

News.title: Households warned of ‘worse to come’ as energy bills rise
News.content:
Households have been warned there is “worse to come” on energy bills after Ofgem raised its price cap to a three-year high.

On Wednesday, the regulator announced typical annual household gas and electricity prices will rise by £60 from October.

The 4pc rise follows a 13pc jump in July as the Iran war pushed up global oil and gas prices.

Analysts at Cornwall Insight, the energy consultancy, said there was no relief in sight for households in January if the conflict in the Middle East continues.

It said a further 9pc rise should be expected in the new year, putting an average January bill up to £1,872 a year, £149 higher than the prices coming into effect from October.

The forecast underlines the challenges faced by Andy Burnham as he stakes his reputation on lowering the cost of living.

Mr Burnham on Wednesday said he recognised rising energy bills were “difficult” for people, adding the government had decided to remove VAT from electricity bills to “give people that little bit of help”.

Speaking to reporters from a supermarket in London, the Prime Minister said: “We know the price cap will have an impact, but it is what we can do right now.

“We’ll continue to look as we go forward at how we get energy prices down in the long term, and that’s what we need to do too.”

However, the latest increase to the price cap effectively wipes out the £45 reduction from Mr Burnham’s VAT cut.

Miatta Fahnbulleh, the Energy Secretary, hinted on Wednesday there could be more action from ministers “to protect families from unaffordable bills”, with the Budget due to be held on October 28.

Commenting on the price cap, Craig Lowrey, of Cornwall Insight, said there was a risk of “more hardship” by January.

“Where January bills land will depend on whether the situation in the Middle East calms down in the next couple of months.”

He added that low European gas stocks heading into the winter meant bills were unlikely to fall.

Elsewhere Ms Fahnbulleh appeared to suggest that investment in net zero projects was contributing to higher household bills.

Asked on LBC if the rise in bills could not solely be blamed on the Middle East conflict, but also on political choices to pay for renewable subsidies, she replied: “Well, no, so it is both.”

However, she later insisted it was “simply not true” that net zero was adding to bills, when questioned by Sky News.

News.title: China clamped down on exotic wildlife farms – now they’ve moved to Southeast Asia
News.content:
We hear the bamboo rats before we see them. At the bottom of almost 200 concrete containers are hundreds of chunky rodents – some squealing as they scurry in circles, others loudly gnawing corn, sugar cane and bamboo with their sharp protruding teeth.

“They’re very easy to keep,” says Suriyan Wanpakwaen, as he peers into one of the pits at the DIY breeding facility beside his home in Nakhon Ratchasima, a province roughly 150 miles northeast of Bangkok. “My favourite thing is how clean they are, there are no bad smells.”

For almost seven years, Mr Suriyan has been farming bamboo rats – and now, the business is booming. A single rodent can sell for as much as 4,000 baht (roughly £90), and there’s so much demand that Mr Suriyan and his wife can’t keep up.

They’re not the only ones cashing in. Since the coronavirus pandemic, backyard wildlife farms like this have proliferated across Southeast Asia.

While this industry long existed in the region, the mounting new additions are filling a vacuum created when, in the wake of Covid-19, China closed thousands of similar farms over bio-security concerns.

“There was obviously a void and therefore an opportunity,” said Dr Ross McEwing, a project officer focused on the illegal wildlife trade and emerging zoonotic diseases at the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) in Bangkok.

“There was a coordinated effort to set up these wildlife farms, led by people who could consolidate stock and move that stock illegally across multiple international borders,” he added.

News.title: Ten years after Brazil’s Zika epidemic, its children are still paying the price
News.content:
In the heated pool, ten-year-old Stephany Vitória Silva Costa is weightless. The water soothes her convulsing muscles, providing brief respite from constant pain, and she coos with delight, igniting smiles among everyone in the room.

Stephany is a “Zika baby”; one of more than 3,080 children born with Congenital Zika Syndrome (CZS) following a devastating outbreak of the mosquito borne virus that swept Brazil in 2015-16. At least 444 of those children have died, mainly from respiratory and infectious diseases.

Like most of the surviving children from the cohort, she has suffered from an array of symptoms including microcephaly, severe cognitive and motor impairment, vision and hearing loss and seizures – which can occur up to ten times a day.

But a decade after the outbreak, a second wave of complications are emerging in children like Stephany.

Stephany’s exposed back, showing the pronounced 120-degree curvature caused by rapid, severe scoliosis Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

As her therapist gently turns her in the pool, a pronounced bulge shows through the back of her pink and blue swim top. Over the last two years, her growing spine has been pulled 120-degrees into an S-shaped curve that is now crushing her lungs.

While many of the children born with microcephaly after the outbreak died in early infancy, a much-loved group including Stephany lived on. Now, however, mortality rates are again climbing as the children near adolescence.

An x-ray image showing a severe s-shaped spinal deformity threatening to compress a young patient’s lungs Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

“It weighs heavily on my heart. After so many years of following these children, it is inevitable to form bonds – not only with them, but with their families,” says Dr Milena Cavalcanti, one of just 11 paediatric neurologists in the state.

“Every loss affects me deeply. It is very hard to say goodbye to them”.

At the Altino Ventura Foundation’s (FAV) hydrotherapy centre, steam clings to murals depicting ocean scenes – a smiling pink octopus swims around a silver painted shipwreck.

As Stephany coos, another girl in a brown swimsuit and rainbow coloured shorts smiles as her mother fills a cup with water and pours it over her black curls.

Originally an ophthalmology institute, FAV expanded into neuro-rehabilitation as the Zika crisis unfolded. It provides free therapy to children with CZS twice a week, with treatment plans reassessed every six months.

Some 230 children affected by the syndrome have had therapy at the foundation and 84 are currently being treated. Its clinicians are tracking the cohort's long-term development.

Physiotherapist Gustav Wagner assists a young patient in the hydrotherapy pool Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

None of the Zika children present can walk or hold themselves up, and the majority have already had at least one major surgery.

Nevertheless, Gustav Wagner, a physiotherapist, says installing the hydrotherapy pool – which increases blood flow and loosens muscles – was a major breakthrough.

The children can’t express pain verbally. Mr Wagner and his team instead use a visual scale from one to ten, based on reading their posture and expressions. The mothers, above all, learn to spot the smallest changes and the pool, they say, makes a huge difference.

Infections early in pregnancy inflicted the worst damage. And in one of the side rooms of the hydrotherapy centre, it's evident that the disabilities are profound.

Five children sit motionless in their wheelchairs with blankets pulled up to their necks. One of them, Emily Sophia dos Santos Luna, weighed just six kilograms at age two before being given a feeding tube to enable her to survive.

She added: “It’s a very difficult life, but God gave us the power to keep going. I will take care of her until the day God wants”.

In the therapeutic gym, a large room filled with foam mats, standing frames and slings hung from the ceiling, Allana Kauane perches on a large silver balance ball.

She wears a green skirt, shin-high pink socks, and a white T-shirt that has “be happy” printed in shimmery lettering.

Ms Rodrigues, her physiotherapist, supports her torso and bounces her gently to build core strength. With every movement, she patiently lifts Allana’s head back up as it falls onto her chest.

Thailene Maria uses a bright gold pompom to draw her daughter’s focus Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

Thailene Maria, the child’s 28-year-old mother, waves a bright gold pompom in front of her eyes in an effort to draw her focus.

Down the corridor in a consultation room, Dr Cavalcanti examines another patient.

It’s a girl who has not had a seizure in six years, but her last one lasted thirty minutes – six times the length that defines a medical emergency in Brazil.

Manuelle does not like to be touched, her grandmother says. She used to bite herself, now she pulls at her own hair instead.

As Dr Cavalcanti taps gently at her knee with a reflex hammer, the girl tenses and struggles to lie flat. Fine dark hair has started to grow along the girl’s shins – a side effect, says Dr Cavalcanti, of the anticonvulsant medication she relies on to control her seizures.

It’s a small reminder that the building was designed to cater for the spiritual needs of its patients alongside their medical care.

While infants with CZS initially received only basic motor stimulation, severe musculoskeletal issues are emerging as they reach adolescence.

Delaying intervention drastically restricts surgical options, Dr Rolim warns.

In the worst cases, repairing the hip is no longer possible. Surgeons must instead remove the top of the thigh bone simply to stop it from grinding against the socket.

Dr Zilda Cavalcanti, Health Secretary of Pernambuco State Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

Ms Sena rarely receives any help with her son Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

“My family doesn’t help me, nobody cares,” she says. “People are afraid of Heytor, they say he’s ‘special’.”

Inside the house, only secured with metal bars on gaping door and window frames, Ms Sena frequently skips meals so Heytor can eat. Ms Sena lifts her son roughly 10 times a day Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

Ms Sena prays for her own robust health so that her son is not without a carer Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

Across Brazil, the mothers of children with Zika are renowned for their resilience.

Many were young and living in poverty when the outbreak hit. Fuelled by deep rooted stigma, most were then abandoned by their partners after their children were born with disabilities.

It took a decade of campaigning for these women – a movement known as the Mothers of Angels – to finally secure the social security breakthrough last year.

They proved that the state failed families twice over: by not containing the virus, and by under-compensating the children for years.

A new generation at risk

It remains unclear whether Brazil is vulnerable to another Zika outbreak.

In 2016, amid the original epidemic, the World Health Organization declared a public health emergency of international concern.

A few months later, cases began to drop and today the population is thought to be protected by herd immunity.

However, that immunity is unlikely to last forever.

A study in Salvador, the capital of nearby Bahia state, found antibody protection dropped from 59 per cent to under 39 per cent within two years of the first outbreak.

Dr Marques estimates Brazil could see another outbreak resulting in children born with CZS within 15 to 20 years.

Originally focused on eye care, the Altino Ventura Foundation expanded its operations during the 2015 outbreak Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

A new generation has grown up without having been exposed to the virus, creating a growing population vulnerable to infection, he says.

The root cause of poor water infrastructure and mosquito infestation also hasn’t been resolved.

“Almost everybody born after 2016 has not been exposed to Zika at all... they are naive, and that piles up with the older people who did not get infected,” he told The Telegraph.

“Once the population vulnerable to Zika reaches a critical threshold, the risk of another outbreak grows”.

The research that could prepare Brazil for that eventuality has stalled.

There is still no approved Zika vaccine or antibody treatment. The most advanced candidate has only just completed early-stage safety trials, and experts say a larger trial is nearly impossible without an active outbreak to test it.

Basic diagnostic tools also have major limitations. Standard antibody tests still cannot reliably distinguish Zika from dengue, and PCR testing – the only definitive testing method – is only effective for around five days at the peak of infections.

For Erika Silva Costa and her ten-year-old daughter Stephany, the child with severe scoliosis, the struggle to secure that necessary care has reached a standstill.

Ms Costa contracted Zika five months into her pregnancy. When doctors recommended that she terminate, she refused.

Erika Silva Costa, Stephany’s mother and full-time caregiver, is also a fierce campaigner Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

A former MRI technician, Ms Costa is now a full-time caregiver and a prominent campaigner for Zika children.

“My dedication to her is total, 24 hours a day… my brain is always awake,” she says, adding that she sleeps in the same bed facing Stephany in case she chokes during the night. “I feel like the umbilical cord was never cut”.

Despite the urgent need, Stephany’s position remains perilous.

Her doctors say she needs an operation costing 150,000 BRL (£21,400) on her spine but so far she has been refused coverage by medical insurers. Ms Costa is now mounting a legal battle to fight the decision in court.

“The authorities together with the health services aren’t tackling this properly,” said Dr Rolim.

“It’s so frustrating. The professionals know what needs to be done, but can’t do it because the system doesn’t provide the right conditions”.

With the public health system crippled by long waiting lists and a lack of specialised equipment, families like Ms Costa are waiting in limbo.

“Sometimes one of the children dies and we all fall apart,” she says. “We have to believe in God to wake up the next day and be strong”.

News.title: Glasner made to wait for first win as Trafford thwarts Forest
News.content:
Leeds manager Daniel Farke said: “He has the potential to be one of the best goalkeepers in the Premier League and that is why Thomas Tuchel has picked him for England.

“I like his natural confidence and aura, he knows that he’s good and he will be outstanding one day.

“He has major chances to be under the spotlight and we are very pleased with him so far.”

Forest manager Oliver Glasner will be pleased to see the back of Leeds. He was appointed by Forest for the primary reason of winning trophies after successful tenures with Crystal Palace and Eintracht Frankfurt, but this particular avenue is now closed for this season.

Four-time League Cup winners, Forest endured a difficult evening following the pre-match news that they have agreed a £45m deal with Chelsea for striker Liam Delap.

Forest have established a reputation for noisy transfer windows but are determined to focus on quality over quantity this year. With Delap to undergo a medical on Wednesday, Forest will then focus on signing a new right wing-back before the deadline.

Newcastle’s Jacob Murphy has been discussed, though a move is now regarded as unlikely. There are understood to be other targets under consideration.

Glasner has insisted he does not want Forest to panic, and it remains to be seen whether they do spring into life on the final day. He said: “I am not a magician or the messiah and we cannot ignore the reality that Leeds are ahead of us at the moment.

Sports.title: Man Utd legend Paul Scholes’ daughter shows off scars in bikini after she was hospitalised
Sports.content:
PAUL SCHOLES’ daughter Alicia has shown off her scars in a bikini snap after being hospitalised.

Alicia, 25, shared a number of holiday pictures after showing herself sunbathing by the pool at a luxury resort.



And she displayed scars around her abdomen in her showreel of photos this week.

Earlier this month she revealed she had been treated at Tameside General Hospital but didn’t declare the reason.



Alicia – who is the second youngest of Manchester United legend Scholes – made light of the scars as she posed for a mirror selfie.

In her caption, she wrote: “Took my 3 brand new shiny scars away.”



She received messages of support in the comments as one fan said: “So pretty.”

Another called her “so gorgeous”.

Alicia has more than 100,000 followers on Instagram and is often seen posting glamorous and revealing snaps.

She is one three children shared by Scholes and ex-wife Claire along with sons Arron and Aiden.



It comes after Alicia opened up about another medical issue after suffering a gruesome toe injury.



She shared pictures of a nasty-looking patch of skin missing from the side of her foot while on another trip with boyfriend Ayo Odukoya and said it was a treadmill-related incident.

And another close-up revealed one of her toes bloodied and badly grazed around the nail.

Alicia – who previously played netball for London Pulse – simply wrote alongside the painful-looking image: “ouch it hurts.”

Fortunately, the injury did not appear to completely ruin her trip as the netball player continued to share pictures from her getaway.

Her latest toe drama comes years after dad Scholes went viral for a rather different reason involving his daughter’s feet.



A bizarre clip shared online in 2021 appeared to show the Manchester United legend nibbling on Alicia’s toenails.

Sports.title: Chelsea in talks with Emiliano Martinez over transfer after they are offered Aston Villa’s World Cup winning keeper
Sports.content:
CHELSEA are tempted to land Emiliano Martinez – after the Aston Villa goalkeeper was pushed in their direction.

The Blues got their season off to a winning start as they narrowly beat Fulham on Monday.



But Chelsea are in talks with Martinez, 33, over a late move from Villa before the transfer window slams shut.

The Argentine has been offered to the West Londoners by the shot-stopper’s representatives.



Martinez is on the market after his switch to Juventus collapsed earlier this month.

The Serie A giants backed away from a deal when Villa held out for £8.5million instead of being prepared to accept £6m plus £2.5m in add-ons.



And Martinez has been left in limbo thanks to his replacement already jetting into the Midlands.

Zion Suzuki headed to Villa in a £30million deal after pulling out of a move to Paris Saint-Germain.

Robert Sanchez was given the nod between the sticks when Chelsea overcame Fulham earlier this week.

But the Spaniard came in for fierce criticism when his blunder gifted the Cottagers a first half equaliser through Josh King.



SUN VEGAS WELCOME OFFER: GET UP TO £100 BONUS

And another error allowed Gonzalo Garcia to give Fulham hope of rescuing a point.

Chelsea have insisted all summer that they are happy with their current goalkeeping options.

But Sanchez’s worrying performance at Craven Cottage has resulted in Blues boss Xabi Alonso considering a late swoop for Martinez.

The former Arsenal man played a key role in Argentina celebrating World Cup glory in 2022.



And he narrowly missed out on repeating the feat when the South American giants lost to Spain in the final this summer.

Chelsea have already landed Morgan Rogers, Maxence Lacroix, Danny Welbeck and Jordan Henderson from Premier League rivals since the transfer window opened.

Sports.title: Man City set to bid for Enzo Fernandez despite missing transfer deadline as Chelsea line up replacement in Alex Scott
Sports.content:
MANCHESTER CITY are preparing an opening bid for Chelsea’s Enzo Fernandez.

The Blues value the midfielder, 25, at more than £120million after their self-imposed August 14 deadline for bids at that price came and went without an offer.



Despite that deadline, City’s interest remains with new boss Enzo Maresca keen on a reunion with the Argentine.

Speaking while on international duty in March, Fernandez criticised the Blues for Maresca’s departure from Stamford Bridge as their season spiralled out of control.



TRANSFER NEWS LIVE: ALL THE LATEST FROM THE SUMMER WINDOW

Chelsea will seek a replacement for Fernandez if an agreement is reached with City and, despite having a £64m bid rejected, they remain keen on Bournemouth’s Alex Scott.

The Cherries have insisted the midfielder, who has rejected the offer of a new contract, is not for sale but Chelsea are prepared to further test their resolve.



Maresca is overhauling City’s midfield, having already signed £116m Elliot Anderson and now added teenager Ayyoub Bouaddi in an £81m deal from Lille confirmed on Wednesday.

Rodri, Bernardo Silva and Tijjani Reijnders have all left while Nico Gonzalez is closing in on a move to Newcastle.

Bouaddi, 18, said: “This is a very special day for me and my family.

“Manchester City are, for me, the best club in the world. It’s a dream to be here and be able to call myself a City player.



BEST FREE BETS AND BETTING SIGN UP OFFERS

“I have spent most of my life working hard to become the best player I can be and reach the top of the game.

“I’ve watched City for many years, and I love their style of play. City always try and play quality football. And they have shown they are winners – this club feels like it’s built to win.”

Chelsea maintain they are happy to keep Fernandez if their valuation is not met, while new manager Xabi Alonso has stated he wants the midfielder to stay.

However, the former Benfica man, signed for a then British transfer record £106m in January 2023, was not named in the starting XI to face Fulham in the Premier League opener on Monday night.

Fernandez was introduced as a second-half substitute and cheered by the travelling fans having been booed at Stamford Bridge during Chelsea’s final pre-season friendly earlier this month.



The current record fee spent by a British club stands at £125m, paid by Liverpool to Newcastle last summer for striker Alexander Isak.

Sports.title: Differential options for Gameweek 2: Featuring Mamadou Sangare and Ben White
Sports.content:
THIS season we will suggest a handful of differential options for Dream Team managers to consider prior to each Gameweek deadline.

By differentials, we mean players who feature in very few teams and therefore have the potential to make a significant impact.

Mamadou Sangare (£3m)

Brentford’s new midfield general provided three assists in Gameweek 1.



He registered two during the Bees’ dismantling of Tottenham and then came off the bench on Tuesday night to set up one of Nathan Collins’s (£3m) goals against Birmingham in the Carabao Cup.



It’s early days but it appears Sangare will be a key player for Keith Andrews both in and out of possession.

Just 1.2% of gaffers took a punt on the ex-Lens midfielder for Gameweek 1 and they were rewarded with a 17-point haul.

Brentford are due to face Leeds at Elland Road this Sunday, a tricky fixture given the Whites’ home record under Daniel Farke, but the West Londoners could not have started better having scored nine goals in their first two outings.



Nathan Collins (£3m), Michael Kayode (£3m) and Vitaly Janelt (£2m) have also started in fine style.

Ben White (£4.5m)

It’s rare to find a viable differential in Arsenal’s ranks as the Premier League champions are generally well backed.

But their No4’s ownership of 3.9% looks low given he is likely to play all the minutes that matter at right-back while Jurrien Timber (£5m) is sidelined with injury.



Granted, Ezri Konsa’s (£4m) arrival may shake up the pecking order but the England regular is a centre-back first and foremost — he’s more likely to take minutes from Cristhian Mosquera (£4.5m).

White is not an entirely risk-free punt but the appeal is obvious; he assisted the Gunners’ third goal against Coventry and matched Riccardo Calafiori’s (£4.5m) haul of 10 points — for comparison the Italian is the second-most popular defender in the game.

Mikel Arteta will be confident of another positive result on Monday night when his side will face Aston Villa at Villa Park given the Villains’ shambolic display at Brighton.

Maxim De Cuyper (£3.5m)

Speaking of the Seagulls, their Belgian full-back was deployed as a left winger against the Villains and justified Fabian Hurzeler’s decision within 18 minutes.



De Cuyper (1% ownership) forced Victor Lindelof (£3m) into an own goal and then popped up in the six-yard box to double Brighton’s lead as Unai Emery’s troops capitulated at the Amex.

And because he’s categorised as a defender, he also banked clean sheet points from the 4-0 win for a total return of 18 points.

De Cuyper’s Gameweek 2 fixture is far from favourable as Chelsea’s front thee looked strong at Fulham on Monday night but out-of-position gems make for powerful assets in the world of Dream Team.

Yoane Wissa (£3m)

Dream Team bosses keen to target a specific fixture should consider Newcastle’s No9.



The DR Congo international played behind William Osula (£3m) against Liverpool but his underlying numbers caught the eye.

Wissa generated 0.94 xG from four shots, made four tackles, won four free-kicks, and provide an assist for Joe Willock (£2.5m).

Up next is a trip to Spurs, who were flattered by a 3-0 defeat to Brentford in their opening game.

Roberto De Zerbi’s side conceded 26 shots worth a whopping 3.96 xG and Newcastle’s attackers will be licking their lips at the prospect of facing such a vulnerable defence — although Pedro Porro (£4m) and Micky van de Ven (£3.5m) are expected to return for the North Londoners.
