The Streak Broke at 2.1%

The July consumer price index came in at 2.1% month-on-month, the INDEC reported on August 13, up two-tenths from June’s 1.9%. It is a small move with outsized symbolism: the monthly path this year — 2.9% in January, 2.9% in February, 3.4% in March, 2.6% in April, 2.1% in May, 1.9% in June — had been a clean disinflation story until July interrupted it.

The cumulative figures frame the political problem. Prices are up 19.3% in the first seven months of 2026 and 33.8% against July 2025.

Milei had told voters the monthly index would start with a zero by August — the official forecast survey now shows no such month anywhere on the horizon.

Seasonals Did the Damage

The composition softens the headline. Core inflation — the measure central bankers watch — ran at 1.8%, below the general index, while seasonal prices surged 4.5% on winter-holiday items: recreation and culture rose 5%, the month’s biggest division, driven by tourism packages and accommodation.

Regulated prices added 2.1%, food rose 2.0%, and clothing actually fell 1.3%.

Buenos Aires City, often a leading indicator, printed 2.9% for July on services and tourism costs — a warning that August’s national number may not fall back quickly even if July’s spike proves seasonal.

Wholesale Prices Tell a Calmer Story

Five days later, the INDEC’s wholesale index offered the government relief: the IPIM rose just 0.8% in July, down from 1.1% in June. Economy Minister Luis Caputo noted it was the lowest monthly reading since May 2025 and the lowest for any July since 2019, and Milei celebrated that July at the wholesale level “started with a zero.”

The details show an anchor and a warning. Crude oil and gas fell 9.2%, dragging the index down, while electricity jumped 5.8% and farm products rose 3.6% — pipeline pressures that could reach consumers by spring.

Wholesale inflation totals 16.6% for the year and 31.1% year-on-year.

What Comes Next

The central bank’s REM survey, published August 6, captures the professional consensus: 2026 closes at 29.8% inflation, the next twelve months at 21.8%, and monthly readings between 1.6% and 1.8% into January 2027. Disinflation continues, in other words — just slower than the president’s book title, The End of Inflation, advertised.

The last mile of any stabilization is always the stickiest; Argentina is now walking it in public.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Argentina’s inflation rate right now?

Consumer prices rose 2.1% in July 2026, the INDEC reported on August 13 — up from 1.9% in June. Inflation totals 19.3% for January–July 2026 and 33.8% measured against July of last year.

Why did Argentina’s inflation accelerate in July 2026?

Mainly seasonal factors: winter-holiday tourism, accommodation and recreation pushed seasonal prices up 4.5%, with recreation and culture rising 5% — the strongest division. Core inflation stayed lower at 1.8%, and wholesale prices rose just 0.8%, suggesting limited underlying pressure.

Will Argentina reach zero monthly inflation in 2026?

Unlikely. The BCRA’s REM survey of banks and consultancies, published August 6, projects monthly inflation between 1.6% and 1.8% into January 2027 and 29.8% for all of 2026 — no zero-comma month appears anywhere on the forecast horizon.

If you have a flight to or from Buenos Aires this week, confirm your airport before you leave the house. Aeroparque is closed until Thursday afternoon and Ezeiza is handling nearly double its normal load.

What is happening and why

Aeroparque Jorge Newbery, Buenos Aires’s downtown airport, is closed for 55 hours from 9 a.m. on Tuesday 25 August to 4 p.m. on Thursday 27 August. The closure is for preventive maintenance on the main runway, including resurfacing work that cannot be done while aircraft are operating.

The airport normally handles about 450 flights per day. Over the 55-hour window, roughly 900 scheduled flights are affected. Airport operator Aeropuertos Argentina 2000 and the civil aviation regulator ANAC coordinated the work months in advance, but the scale of the disruption is still significant — particularly for domestic passengers who rely on Aeroparque’s convenience.

Which flights are moving where

About 540 flights have been moved to Ezeiza Ministro Pistarini, the city’s main international airport 35 kilometres southwest of the centre. Another 360 have been rescheduled to operate before or after the closure window.

The airlines have handled the reallocation differently. Aerolíneas Argentinas, the dominant carrier, has consolidated most of its domestic network at Ezeiza. JetSmart has formally announced suspensions of some services and is offering rebooking. Flybondi, the low-cost carrier, has shifted its Buenos Aires operations entirely to Ezeiza for the duration. LATAM, GOL, Andes, Avianca and Paranair have each published revised schedules.

The practical effect is that Ezeiza — designed for long-haul international traffic — is handling roughly 940 flights across the closure period, against a normal load of about 530. That is an 80 percent increase that will stretch check-in, security, baggage handling and immigration.

What you should do

Confirm your departure airport. Do not assume your flight is from Aeroparque just because that is where it usually departs. Check your booking confirmation, the airline’s app or website, or call the airline directly. Some passengers are discovering the closure only at the terminal door.

Allow far more time for Ezeiza. The airport is an hour from the city centre in good traffic, versus 15 minutes for Aeroparque. With the increased load, security queues and check-in waits will be longer than normal. Arrive three hours before a domestic departure and four hours before an international one.

Consider ground transport carefully. The Manuel Tienda León bus service from downtown to Ezeiza runs every 30 minutes and takes 50–70 minutes depending on traffic. Taxis and ride-hailing apps cost roughly ARS 45,000–60,000 at the wholesale rate, or about US$30–40. The urban train to Ezeiza exists but is slow and involves a connection; it is not recommended with luggage during this period.

If you are connecting, be aware that Aerolíneas Argentinas and some other carriers are operating split terminals at Ezeiza — domestic flights from Terminal C and international from Terminal A. The shuttle bus between terminals runs every 10 minutes but allow 30 minutes for a comfortable connection.

When things return to normal

Aeroparque reopens at 4 p.m. on Thursday 27 August. The first scheduled departures are domestic evening services to Córdoba, Mendoza and Bariloche. By Friday 28 August the schedule should be back to normal, though some airlines may need 24–48 hours to reposition aircraft and crews.

If your flight was cancelled and you have not been rebooked, Argentine consumer protection law entitles you to a full refund or rebooking at no extra cost. The airline must provide meals and accommodation if the cancellation forces an overnight stay. Document everything and file a complaint with the National Directorate for Consumer Defence if the airline refuses.

When does Aeroparque reopen?

At 4 p.m. on Thursday 27 August 2026. The first departures are domestic evening services. By Friday 28 August the schedule should be back to normal.

Can I still fly to Buenos Aires during the closure?

Yes, but your flight will land at Ezeiza, not Aeroparque. All arrivals are being redirected. Allow extra time for ground transport into the city — Ezeiza is an hour away in good traffic.

What if my flight was cancelled?

You are entitled to a full refund or free rebooking under Argentine consumer protection law. If the cancellation forces an overnight stay, the airline must provide meals and accommodation. Document everything and file a complaint with the National Directorate for Consumer Defence if the airline refuses.

01 Argentine Markets: The Peso Crawl Continues

Argentina is still the dominant story. The wholesale peso closed Tuesday at 1,512 per US dollar, up five pesos from Monday’s first-ever break above 1,500 and its fourth consecutive daily nominal record. The move is small in percentage terms — about 0.3 percent — but the direction is unmistakable. The retail official rate went to 1,530, the blue held steady at 1,560 and the contado con liquidación sat around 1,600.

The Buenos Aires stock market defended the 3 million line. The S&P Merval rose 0.8 percent to 3,009,029 points, its third straight session of gains, after dipping below the 3 million mark intraday. Utilities led: Transener jumped 5.8 percent and Transportadora de Gas del Norte rose 3.3 percent. Bank Supervielle added 2.9 percent.

YPF was the outlier, falling 2.1 percent after a fatal accident at its Rincón del Mangrullo block in the Vaca Muerta shale formation. The state oil firm is the heaviest weight in the index, so its drop dragged even as the broader board rose.

Country risk — the premium investors demand over US Treasuries to hold Argentine paper — was last published at 509 basis points on Monday 24 August, up from 505 on Friday 21 August. The widening through the month reflects bond-market nervousness about the fiscal path even as the crawling peg continues.

What it means for you. If you are paid in dollars and living in Buenos Aires, the slow peso erosion is steadily increasing your purchasing power in local-currency terms. The wholesale rate is what matters for most large transactions; at 1,512, a US$1,000 transfer buys roughly ARS 1,512,000 at the wholesale window, against ARS 1,560,000 on the blue. The gap has narrowed to about 3 percent, the tightest in months.

Brazil. The Ibovespa jumped 1.55 percent to 174,577 on Tuesday, helped by expectations that Wednesday’s IPCA-15 inflation preview will be soft. The central bank cut the Selic to 14.00 percent in August and the market is debating whether one more quarter-point ease is coming at the September 15–16 Copom meeting. A soft core services reading today would strengthen that case. The IPCA-15 print lands at 9 a.m. Brasília time.

Chile. The peso barely moved at 913.30 per dollar while the S&P IPSA fell 0.8 percent to 11,451, dragged down by lithium producer SQM-B dropping 4.1 percent on talk of a major Chinese mine restarting. Copper — the traditional anchor — was not the driver. The index remains about 1.5 percent below its record high near 11,628.

Mexico. The peso firmed to 16.9460 on the FIX after weakening to 16.9647 on Monday’s inflation print. The S&P/BMV IPC rose 0.79 percent to 66,293, back above the 66,000 level. Banxico is on hold at 6.50 percent and the minutes point to staying there; the 3 percent inflation target is now expected in the fourth quarter of 2027.

03 Visas, Residency & Tax

Where What changed What it means for you Region-wide Nothing new this week. No visa, residency, fee, appointment or court change surfaced in Brazil, Mexico, Argentina, Chile, Peru, Uruguay or Costa Rica between 18 and 26 August. Worth saying plainly. Also worth a warning: several aggregator sites are running headlines claiming Brazil, Mexico, Colombia, Chile and Peru will bar foreigners over passport validity. There is no primary source behind any of them. Ignore. Colombia The permanent-visa transfer deadline under Resolución 9316 of 2024 stands at 31 October 2026. The salvoconducto requirement has been dropped. Nine weeks left. Without the transfer, Migración Colombia will not issue your cédula de extranjería. Do not leave it to October. Colombia The structural tax reform is still a pledge. The government has confirmed September and has said it will not fund earthquake recovery with new taxes. The plan targets tax breaks that grew from about COP 68 trillion in 2019 to more than COP 136 trillion in 2023, roughly US$22 billion to US$45 billion at today’s rate. The 183-day tax-residency test is unchanged. If the bill lands as described, the change for foreign residents is the removal of exemptions rather than a headline rate move. Panama Standing deadline, now inside seven weeks: the US$300,000 real-estate route to day-one permanent residence runs until 15 October 2026, after which the threshold rises to US$500,000. If you were considering it, the window is closing and the difference is US$200,000.

04 Getting Around

Buenos Aires: Aeroparque is shut for a second day. The city airport closed at 9 a.m. on Tuesday and reopens at 4 p.m. on Thursday 27 August, 55 hours in total, for preventive work on the main runway. Today is the middle day — when the most disruption hits travellers who missed yesterday’s warnings. Roughly 900 flights are affected: about 540 have been moved to Ezeiza and 360 rescheduled. Ezeiza goes from around 530 flights in a normal window to about 940, an increase of roughly 80 percent. Aerolíneas Argentinas, JetSmart, Flybondi, LATAM, GOL, Andes, Avianca and Paranair are all affected.

The practical instruction is the same as yesterday: confirm your departure airport, not just your time, before you set out, and allow far more time than usual for Ezeiza, which is an hour from the city rather than fifteen minutes. If your flight was originally from Aeroparque and has not been rescheduled, check with your airline — some passengers are only discovering the closure at the terminal door.

Colombia: Pereira’s Matecaña reopens today. The airport resumes commercial operations after its 10 August earthquake closure. LATAM resumes with two daily flights from Bogotá and one from Medellín, 21 a week, against five daily before the earthquake — so the schedule will be thin for weeks. One local outlet had reported a 25 August reopening; every other source, including LATAM, confirms the 26th. The terminal building has been inspected and cleared, but some secondary facilities are still being repaired. Confirm with your airline before travelling.

Paraguay: The central bank meets today for its monthly rate decision. The benchmark has been 5.5 percent since July and the market expects no change, but confirm the timing with the BCP if you have financial commitments tied to the rate.

05 Weather & Safety

Rio is unstable today with a maximum around 21°C and a high chance of rain. August has already delivered 65 millimetres to the 24th, which is 186 percent of the monthly normal — this has been a wet month by any measure. Buenos Aires is cold and partly sunny, 7 to 12°C today. The national weather service has no precipitation for the city until Thursday.

The Servicio Meteorológico Nacional has orange and yellow warnings today for snow, wind and rain across several Argentine provinces. Metropolitan Buenos Aires is not under an extreme-weather warning, though a cold-temperature alert remains active. No active INMET alert was confirmed for Rio or São Paulo.

On advisories, the United States has Colombia at Level 3, Reconsider Travel, on an advisory dated 31 March 2026 that has not been reissued since the August earthquake; Level 4 Do Not Travel still covers Arauca, Cauca outside Popayán, Valle del Cauca outside Cali, Norte de Santander and the ten-kilometre strip along the Venezuelan border. The British Foreign Office advises against all but essential travel within five kilometres of the Colombia–Ecuador border, except the Rumichaca and Ipiales crossings; its earlier border-closure text was removed in June. Separately, Bolivia has been under a state of emergency since 20 June, declared by President Rodrigo Paz, giving the military powers to clear road blockades — worth knowing if you are travelling overland.

The earthquake and the closure

The 10 August earthquake, centred near the Quindío-Pereira border, caused structural damage to Matecaña’s terminal building and surface cracking on parts of the apron and taxiways. The airport was immediately closed to commercial traffic while engineers from the Aeronáutica Civil de Colombia assessed the damage.

Initial estimates suggested a closure of one to two weeks, but the damage to secondary facilities — including the baggage handling system and parts of the firefighting infrastructure — extended the shutdown to 16 days. The main runway was cleared within a week, but terminal repairs and safety recertification took longer.

What is flying now

LATAM, the only major carrier serving Matecaña, resumes today with a reduced schedule: two daily flights from Bogotá and one from Medellín, totalling 21 weekly services. Before the earthquake, the airline operated five daily flights — roughly 35 weekly — so capacity is down by about 40 percent.

The reduced schedule reflects both the physical constraints of the terminal — some gates are still out of service — and LATAM’s cautious approach to demand recovery. The airline has said it will add flights “as operational conditions permit,” but has not given a timeline for full restoration.

Other carriers, including Avianca and budget airline Ultra Air, have not announced restart dates. Ultra Air had only recently begun Pereira services before the earthquake and may delay relaunching until the terminal is fully restored.

What to expect on arrival

The terminal building has been inspected and cleared for passenger use, but some areas remain cordoned off for repairs. Travellers should expect temporary signage, some construction noise, and possible delays while the reduced staff and equipment handle the load.

Baggage claim may be slower than usual. The main carousel was undamaged but the secondary system is still being repaired, so large bags may be handled manually. Allow extra time if you are connecting to ground transport.

Ground transport from the airport to Pereira city centre — about 7 kilometres — is operating normally. Taxis, ride-hailing apps and hotel shuttles are available. The bus to Armenia and Manizales has resumed its regular schedule.

Alternatives if you cannot get a flight

If the thin schedule does not work for your dates, the nearest alternatives are Armenia’s El Edén airport (about 45 minutes by road) and Manizales’s La Nubia (about 90 minutes). Both are smaller than Matecaña and have limited service, but they may offer options.

El Edén has daily Avianca flights from Bogotá and occasional service from Medellín. La Nubia is restricted to small aircraft because of its mountain location and has only a few weekly flights. The overland route from Bogotá — about 270 kilometres — takes roughly six hours by bus or four hours by car on good roads, though landslide risk in the Quindío Pass requires checking conditions after heavy rain.

Is Matecaña airport fully operational?

The terminal is open for passengers and the runway is clear, but some secondary facilities are still being repaired. The schedule is thin and some gates remain out of service. Expect temporary signage and possible delays.

Which airlines are flying to Pereira?

LATAM resumes today with 21 weekly flights — two daily from Bogotá and one from Medellín. Avianca and Ultra Air have not announced restart dates. Before the earthquake, LATAM operated five daily flights.

What are the alternatives if I cannot get a flight to Pereira?

Armenia’s El Edén airport is about 45 minutes away and has daily Avianca flights from Bogotá. Manizales’s La Nubia is 90 minutes but limited to small aircraft. The bus from Bogotá takes about six hours on good roads; check for landslides after rain.

World.title: Ecuador Approves Law Letting Military Aid Police Without Emergency
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Ecuador · SECURITY

Key Facts — Law Organic law regulating complementary Armed Forces support to the National Police under Article 158

— Vote 83 in favor, 63 against, 3 abstentions on 25 August 2026

— Scope drug trafficking, terrorism, extortion, illegal mining and prison crises

— Limits deployments capped at 180 days, renewable once for 30 days

— Next step bill goes to President Noboa for signature or veto

The 83-vote approval implements a 2024 referendum mandate and ends Quito’s reliance on rolling emergency decrees, but critics say key controls were cut.

Ecuador’s National Assembly on Tuesday, 25 August 2026, approved a long-delayed law that allows the Armed Forces to support the National Police in fighting organized crime without the president having to declare a state of emergency. The Ecuador military support law passed its second and final debate with 83 votes in favor, 63 against and three abstentions, and will now be sent to President Daniel Noboa, who can sign it into law or veto it.

Ecuadorian soldiers on patrol; a new law regulates military support to police without emergency decrees.

What the Ecuador Military Support Law Allows

The bill, formally called the Organic Law Regulating the Complementary and Subsidiary Support of the Armed Forces to the National Police, develops Article 158 of the Constitution, which Ecuadorians reformed in an April 2024 referendum. It contains 20 articles plus general, reform and transitory provisions, including amendments to the law on the legitimate use of force and to the public and state security law. Under the Ecuador military support law, troops can back the police only when the force’s operational capacity has been objectively and demonstrably overwhelmed by a specific threat.

The law restricts military support to a closed list of crimes written into the Constitution: drug trafficking, terrorism, money laundering, arms and human trafficking, illegal mining, extortion, intimidation and organized crime, as well as grave internal disturbances in the prison system. It states that the Armed Forces will not replace the police or assume ordinary public security duties permanently, and that activation does not in itself suspend constitutional rights. The support provided for in this law ‘does not require an internal armed conflict, does not in itself constitute a state of emergency and does not imply the suspension of constitutional rights,’ ruling-party lawmaker Inés Alarcón, who sponsored the bill, told the chamber, adding that it does not create powers or modify the competences of either institution.

How Military Support Will Be Activated

The Ecuador military support law sets out a fixed chain of steps before a single soldier can deploy. The process starts with a motivated, documented request from the general commander of the National Police to the president, specifying the territory, the crimes targeted and why police capabilities have been exceeded. The Joint Command of the Armed Forces then has 48 hours to produce a technical report on the need, relevance and scope of the support. Within 24 hours the president must convene the Public and State Security Council (Cosepe) to approve a definitive report, and the head of state has a further 48 hours to issue the decree.

Safeguards continue after the decree is signed. The executive must notify the Constitutional Court and the National Assembly within 24 hours so both can exercise subsequent oversight. Deployments are capped at 180 days, renewable once for up to 30 additional days if the original causes persist, and a renewal request must be filed at least 10 days before the initial period expires; support can also be ended early. The text adds rules on operational coordination between police and soldiers and requires human rights and legitimate-use-of-force training for personnel involved in joint operations. For prison crises, the request must also draw on information from the technical body of the social rehabilitation system.

Who Backed the Law and Who Opposed It

The bill cleared its second and final debate with 83 votes in favor from Noboa’s Acción Democrática Nacional (ADN), the Social Christian Party (PSC) and independents aligned with the executive. The 63 lawmakers of the opposition Revolución Ciudadana, the party of former president Rafael Correa, voted against, while three legislators from the Indigenous movement Pachakutik abstained.

Opposition lawmakers said they did not reject military cooperation itself, which seven in ten voters endorsed at the ballot box, but rather the final wording. Revolución Ciudadana assembly member Paola Cabezas said provisions in the first-debate report had disappeared from the text that was voted on, removing oversight of possible excesses in the use of force, rules on the progressive use of force and guarantees for peaceful protest, while widening the secrecy surrounding military operations. PSC lawmaker Alfredo Serrano also flagged differences, noting that an obligation for the president to report to the Assembly and the Constitutional Court and complaint mechanisms before the Ombudsman’s Office had been cut. Even so, he said he considered 95 percent of the project positive, and his party voted it through.

From Referendum to Law: A Two-Year Delay

The Ecuador military support law implements a mandate voters delivered more than two years ago. On 21 April 2024, 72.24 percent of voters approved a partial reform of Article 158 of the Constitution to allow complementary military support for the police. A transitory provision gave the Assembly 200 days to pass the implementing rules, but the process took more than 600 days, and the full chamber held the first debate only on 7 January 2026.

In the absence of the legal framework, President Noboa has relied on successive states of emergency to put soldiers on the streets, measures that suspend certain rights and require Constitutional Court review. In January 2024 he went further, declaring an internal armed conflict against 22 criminal gangs his government labels terrorists. Despite the militarized strategy, violence has kept climbing: local outlet Vistazo reported that 2025 closed with a record 9,283 homicides, the worst annual figure in the country’s history.

What Happens Next

The approved text now passes to the executive. Noboa can sign it, object to it in part or veto it outright; if signed, the Ecuador military support law takes effect once published in the Registro Oficial, the official gazette. A veto is considered unlikely, since the bill was sponsored by the chair of the Assembly’s Security Committee, a lawmaker from the president’s own party, and the government has repeatedly urged the legislature to deliver the framework.

The law is a central piece of Noboa’s security policy, which has made military deployment against organized crime its hallmark, alongside a push for foreign security cooperation and tougher sentencing. The vote came one day after Ecuador’s anti-mafias law, which sets prison penalties for gang membership, was published in the Official Register. Supporters argue the new framework replaces open-ended emergency rule with a regulated, time-limited tool; critics counter that it entrenches the military’s role in public security while weakening the controls lawmakers had originally drafted.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Ecuador military support law? It is an organic law approved by Ecuador’s National Assembly on 25 August 2026 that regulates how the Armed Forces can provide complementary and subsidiary support to the National Police against organized crime, without requiring a state of emergency. It implements a constitutional reform backed by 72.24 percent of voters in an April 2024 referendum. Does the law suspend constitutional rights? No. According to its sponsors, military support under the law does not by itself constitute a state of emergency or suspend constitutional guarantees. Deployments are limited to specific serious crimes, capped at 180 days with a single 30-day renewal, and must be notified to the Constitutional Court and the National Assembly within 24 hours. When does the Ecuador military support law take effect? The bill was sent to President Daniel Noboa, who may sign it, partially object to it or veto it. If signed, it enters into force upon publication in the Registro Oficial, and the government has pressed for the framework for months.

World.title: 19-year-old man remanded for allegedly stabbing brother in the eye; come to court with his eye black
World.content:
19-year-old man remanded for allegedly stabbing brother in the eye; come to court with his eye black

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 19-year-old Belize City man has been remanded to the Belize Central Prison after being accused of attacking his older brother with a knife during a family dispute.

Brenton Conrad Archer, a construction worker of Iguana Street, appeared unrepresented in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court, where he was charged with aggravated assault with a dangerous instrument upon his 22-year-old brother.

Archer pleaded not guilty.

Police allege that Archer and his brother became involved in an altercation at a residence on Iguana Street on Friday, August 21. The confrontation reportedly escalated into a fight during which Archer’s brother was stabbed several times.

Police later visited the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital, where the brother was observed with lacerations to both sides of his mouth as well as stab wounds to his left eye and cheek.

The prosecution did not object to bail for Archer; however, the Magistrate expressed concern that the brothers may live at the same residence or in close proximity to each other.

Archer told the court that his brother does not live in the same yard, but the Magistrate opted to temporarily withhold bail while the prosecution verifies their living arrangements.

The court said the precaution was necessary to avoid another confrontation between the siblings once Archer is released.

Archer, who also appeared in court with visible injuries to his eye and a bandaged right hand, was remanded to the Belize Central Prison.

He is due back in court on September 2, 2026, when the issue of bail is expected to be revisited.

World.title: Sheffan Hemmans, Alberto Arreaza remanded over alleged armed burglary and theft of $46,000 pickup
World.content:
Sheffan Hemmans, Alberto Arreaza remanded over alleged armed burglary and theft of $46,000 pickup

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A member of the Belize Coast Guard and a salesman/manager were remanded to the Belize Central Prison on Tuesday after being charged with aggravated burglary in connection with an alleged armed home invasion in Hattieville.

Twenty-nine-year-old Sheffan Devan Hemmans, a member of the Belize Coast Guard, and 46-year-old Alberto Arreaza, a salesman, manager and farmer from Teakettle Village, appeared before a Magistrate in Court #5, where they were jointly charged with aggravated burglary.

Police allege that on Thursday, August 20, the men, while armed with a firearm, entered a home in the Mile 17 area of Hattieville and stole a pickup truck.

The vehicle is valued at $46,000.

Both men pleaded not guilty to the charge.

The Magistrate informed Arreaza and Hemmans that, because the alleged offence involved a firearm, the lower court could not grant them bail at this stage. They were advised that they may apply to the High Court for bail through an attorney if they wish to secure their release before becoming eligible for bail consideration in the Magistrate’s Court.

Both men were subsequently remanded to the Belize Central Prison.

Arreaza and Hemmans are due back in court on October 20, 2026, when they are expected to receive disclosure in the case.

World.title: Man accused of stealing cousin’s bicycle remanded after court rejects guilty plea
World.content:
Man accused of stealing cousin’s bicycle remanded after court rejects guilty plea

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 27-year-old Belize City construction worker accused of stealing his cousin’s bicycle was remanded to the Belize Central Prison after telling the court he was considering pleading guilty simply because he had no one to bail him.

Israel Anthony Usher appeared unrepresented in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court, where he was charged with theft.

Police allege that on August 13, 2026, Usher stole a 24-inch Hurricane Beach Cruiser bicycle valued at $500 from a female relative at a Benbow Street address.

Before entering a plea, Usher told the Magistrate that if he pleaded not guilty he had no one to secure bail for him, and asked whether pleading guilty would result in a fine instead.

The Magistrate told Usher that a guilty plea could only be accepted if he was actually admitting that he stole the bicycle.

Usher then denied stealing it, telling the court that the owner is his cousin and had allowed him to borrow the bicycle. According to Usher, police later stopped him while he was riding the bicycle against the flow of traffic and confiscated it after he was unable to produce proof of ownership.

He claimed his cousin later believed he had stolen or disposed of the bicycle and made a theft complaint against him.

After hearing his explanation, the Magistrate refused to accept a guilty plea merely for convenience and entered a not-guilty plea on his behalf.

Usher was offered bail in the sum of $500 plus one surety of the same amount, but was unable to secure bail by the end of the day and was remanded to the Belize Central Prison.

He is due back in court on October 6, 2026, when the theft matter will continue.

World.title: Belize City man ordered to stay 100 yards from brother after allegedly pulling knife on him
World.content:
Belize City man ordered to stay 100 yards from brother after allegedly pulling knife on him

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Belize City businessman accused of assaulting his brother, including allegedly threatening him with a knife, is out on bail but has been ordered by the court to stay at least 100 yards away from his sibling while the case remains active.

Thirty-two-year-old Alexander Elvis Jones, a resident of the Conch Shell Bay area, appeared unrepresented in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court, where he was charged with common assault and aggravated assault with a dangerous instrument upon his brother.

The charges stem from an alleged dispute on August 5, 2026.

Jones pleaded not guilty to both counts.

With no objection from the prosecution, the Magistrate granted him bail in the sum of $1,000 plus one surety of the same amount.

As conditions of his bail, Jones must have no contact with his brother or any other prosecution witnesses and must remain at least 100 yards away from the complainant. He is also required to attend all court dates or risk having his bail revoked.

Jones met bail and is due back in court on October 5, 2026, for disclosure.

World.title: Woman granted $800 bail after allegedly threatening to burn down her sister’s home with sister and children inside
World.content:
Woman granted $800 bail after allegedly threatening to burn down her sister’s home with sister and children inside

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 38-year-old Belize City woman has been granted bail after being charged with threat to damage property following an alleged family dispute in which she is accused of threatening to burn down her sister’s home.

Shantae Robateau, a customer care representative, appeared in court unrepresented and pleaded not guilty to the charge. Police allege that during an incident on July 31, 2026, Robateau threatened her sister, saying she would burn down the house while she and her children were inside.

According to the police report, the sister told investigators that she was at her Ebony Street home at around 9:15 p.m. when Robateau allegedly arrived outside the residence carrying a piece of 2-by-4 wood, shouting and demanding that Jones come outside.

The complainant reportedly contacted their older brother, who lives nearby, and asked him to intervene. Police say that as efforts were made to remove Robateau from the property, she allegedly threatened to physically harm her sister and later threatened to burn the house down with her sister and her children inside.

The woman subsequently made a report to police, prompting an investigation. Robateau later turned herself in to police and was charged.

At her arraignment, the prosecution did not object to bail but requested that conditions be imposed. The Magistrate granted Robateau bail in the sum of $800 with one surety of the same amount.

As part of her bail conditions, she must report to the Raccoon Street Police Station every Friday between 6:00 a.m. and 6:00 p.m. and attend all scheduled court appearances.

The case was adjourned until October 13, 2026.

World.title: Justin Goff rejects 1 year sentence for guilty plea in ammunition case
World.content:
Justin Goff rejects 1 year sentence for guilty plea in ammunition case

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Justin Stephen Goff, 38, has decided to maintain his not guilty plea and proceed toward trial on a charge of keeping unlicensed ammunition, two days after asking the Belize City Magistrate’s Court for an indication of the sentence he could receive if he pleaded guilty.

Goff appeared in court Friday morning and told the Magistrate that, after considering the matter, he would not plead guilty.

On Wednesday, August 19, Goff had requested a sentence indication as he considered changing his plea. He was reportedly informed that, after consideration of an early guilty plea and other mitigating and aggravating factors, he could face a sentence of approximately one year and four months’ imprisonment.

Goff, however, rejected that option on Friday and will instead contest the charge.

His case was adjourned until September 4, 2026, when he is expected to receive disclosure from the prosecution.

Goff was first arraigned on April 7, 2026, after police alleged that he was found three days earlier in possession of three live rounds of ammunition — two S&B rounds and one Aguila round — without a licence.

At his arraignment, Goff pleaded not guilty and alleged that the ammunition had been planted on him by a police officer. He told the court that he had been asleep beneath a shed when officers approached and questioned him about a firearm.

Goff claimed that an officer later produced three rounds of ammunition and falsely attributed them to him.

He remains on remand while the case proceeds.

World.title: Protecting Belize’s Children: UNHCR and UNICEF train social workers to handle high-risk cases
World.content:
Protecting Belize’s Children: UNHCR and UNICEF train social workers to handle high-risk cases

By Zoila Palma: UNHCR, the UN Refugee Agency, and UNICEF are working to strengthen Belize’s child protection system by training social workers and child protection professionals to better respond to vulnerable children, including those affected by displacement, abuse, neglect and family separation.

The Best Interest Procedure Training brings together frontline professionals from across the country to develop practical skills for making decisions that prioritize the safety, rights and well-being of children.

Participants are taking part in case studies, interactive discussions and practical exercises focused on assessing risks and developing appropriate protection responses.

The training is especially important for cases involving violence, exploitation, neglect, abuse, displacement and family separation, where decisions can have lasting consequences for children.

The Best Interest Procedure provides a structured, child-centered approach to help social workers determine what course of action is most appropriate for each individual child.

The initiative forms part of continued collaboration between UNHCR, UNICEF and the Department of Human Services within the Ministry of Human Development, Family Support and Gender Affairs.

UNHCR Officer-in-Charge in Belize Mariya Voloshkevich said strengthening the capacity of social workers is an important investment in Belize’s child protection system, while UNICEF Representative Sajid Ali emphasized that every child has the right to protection, care and support.

Department of Human Services Director Shawn Vargas stressed that family separation must be approached with particular care. He noted that children have a fundamental right to family life and, whenever it is safe and appropriate, should remain with or maintain meaningful contact with their families. He emphasized that separation should not be treated as an easy or automatic solution, and that any decision to separate a child from their family must be lawful, necessary and proportionate, while considering both the immediate and long-term impact on the child.

UNHCR and UNICEF say they will continue working with Belizean officials and partners to strengthen child protection services and safeguard the rights and well-being of children across the country.

World.title: Imari Young keeps bail after missing court date, trial set for October
World.content:
Imari Young keeps bail after missing court date, trial set for October

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Fresh Pond resident Imari Young, who is before the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on a burglary charge, was allowed to remain on bail Friday after being brought before the court on a bench warrant for failing to attend a previous court date.

Young appeared unrepresented before Magistrate Neeshad Rohammad, who asked him to explain why his bail should not be revoked after he failed to appear in court on July 22.

Young told the court that he had been sick at the time. He also said his mother is hospitalized and that his father recently died. Young claimed that he had obtained a doctor’s document explaining his absence, although the court reportedly had no record of receiving it.

Despite the missed appearance, the Magistrate did not revoke Young’s bail and allowed him to remain free while his case continues.

Young is charged with burglary and is now scheduled to return to the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on October 14, 2026, when his trial is expected to begin.

World.title: Unhealthy trend: Student obesity surges to 15.3%
World.content:
The Global School-based Health Survey confirmed fears that there has been an increase in the number of Jamaican students getting obese and overweight. (Photo: Adobe stock)

MORE than three in every 10 students captured in a recent survey by the National Council on Drug Abuse (NCDA) were overweight while 15.3 per cent of them were obese.

The Global School-based Health Survey (GSHS), which was conducted between January and March this year, had 3,058 respondents from 32 schools, with 76 per cent participation among students and 100 per cent from schools.

It confirmed fears that there has been an increase in the number of Jamaican students getting obese and overweight, while underweight remains a concern.

According to the survey, obesity moved from six per cent in 2010 to 15.3 per cent in 2026, while the number of overweight students jumped from 21.7 per cent in 2010 to 31.7 per cent in 2026.

At the same time, there was an uptick in underweight students, from 2.1 per cent in 2010 to 3.4 per cent in 2026.

The survey also found a dip in physical activity from 23.2 per cent in 2017 to 19.6 per cent in 2026, while 70.2 per cent reported less than eight hours of sleep, which can be attributed to the long hours students spend on the Internet as sedentary behaviour — sitting down for more than three hours per day increased from 56.4 per cent in 2017 to 68 per cent in 2026.

“Students [who are] less active, more sedentary, and many not getting enough sleep means that there is an increased risk of obesity, chronic diseases, poor academic performance, and mental health problems,” said the NCDA.

It called for more physical activity, greater promotion of recreation and sports, and encouragement for students to adopt healthy sleep habits.

The NCDA blamed unhealthy eating patterns for the rise in obesity among students, and recommended the promotion of healthy school food environment, expansion of nutrition education, and promotion of balanced diets.

But despite the increase in obesity and overweight, the survey found that in the 30 days before it was conducted there was a drop in consumption of one or more sodas per day by students.

In 2010 the NCDA found that 72.5 per cent on the respondents had consumed one or more sodas in the 30 days before the survey, while this year only 49.7 per cent of the respondents said they had done so in the past seven days.

The survey said underweight was highest among grade nine boys, 6.4 per cent, and grade 11 girls, 4.8 per cent.

Meanwhile, the highest rate of obesity was among grade seven girls, 43.2 per cent, and grade seven boys, 40.5 per cent.

The Global School-based Health Survey, noted the NCDA, provides high-quality data to inform decision-making and action for school and youth health.

In his reaction to the survey findings, Minister of Health and Wellness Dr Christopher Tufton urged parents and guardians to ensure their children eat healthy foods at home and school.

He said it is always a better choice to take a meal from home to school if the school does not have facilities for the preparation of hot meals.

Tufton also urged parents and guardians to encourage their children to participate in more physical activities if they want to ensure that they do not fall victim to diabetes, heart disease, and other non-communicable diseases.

“Parents and guardians must insist that their children become more health conscious. Fast food and sugary beverages are not healthy, and I want to remind you parents that, should these young ones get diagnosed with a non-communicable disease, it will follow them into adulthood and put more stress on your resources as well as the health system,” said Tufton.

The NCDA said the survey has shown that healthy eating, regular physical activities, and adequate sleep are essential for the well-being, learning, and long-term health of Jamaica’s children and adolescents.

It added that the lack of physical activity increases the risk of obesity, chronic diseases, poor academic performance, and mental health problems.

The GSHS is an international gold-standard survey developed by World Health Organization, in collaboration with United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF); United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO); United States Agency for International Development (USAID); and the United States-based Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

It measures health behaviours and protective factors among students 13 to 17 years of age and is used in 110 countries.

World.title: A different route for boys
World.content:
In this video grab Seargeant Kevin Wallace, dean of discipline and drill instructor at the Jamaica Constabulary Force Cadet Academy, inspects trainees during muster.Video: Jamaica Constabulary Force

As Jamaica continues to grapple with the persistent underperformance of boys in school, the Jamaica Constabulary Force (JCF) is offering an alternative path that combines academics, discipline, and mentorship to help young men find their footing.

The JCF Cadet Academy, established in September 2021, was born out of the police force’s experience working with young people through its Safe Schools Programme and other youth initiatives where cops observed particular challenges among boys, including truancy.

Speaking on the JCF’s Force4Good podcast, principal of the academy Deputy Superintendent of Police Tanecia Johnson said the force recognised the need for a setting where it could provide more focused support to young men.

“When those reports come in, it’s always about the boys outnumbering the girls in terms of truancy and so on, and so as a force… we decided that something must be done in terms of having a better structure to have these boys in an area where we can have that direct concentration,” she said.

The academy now combines traditional schooling with a highly structured boarding environment, with police, trained teachers, guidance counsellors, and other staff working closely with the students.

Johnson said the academy’s approach is based on more than discipline, with staff seeking to understand the circumstances affecting each student and build relationships that encourage them to open up.

“Oftentimes in the schools the students will tell us as the police, as their mentors, as their motivators, things that they will not tell a school principal, things that they will not tell their parents,” she revealed.

Those conversations, Johnson said, allow the academy to address issues such as anger, identity, purpose, attitude and a student’s plans for the future.

The approach is producing encouraging academic results.

This year’s Caribbean Secondary Education Certificate (CSEC) performance included a 100 per cent pass rate in information technology and physical education and sports, while human and social biology recorded 98 per cent, English A 92 per cent, and office administration 90 per cent. Mathematics recorded a 75 per cent pass rate.

At the Caribbean Advanced Proficiency Examination (CAPE) level, communication studies recorded an 88 per cent pass rate, information technology 93 per cent, law – unit one 84 per cent, and law – unit two 75 per cent. Johnson said the results represent the academy’s best academic performance since it was established.

For Johnson, however, the results are only part of what the academy is trying to achieve.

She recalled the experience of a 17-year-old student who arrived after struggling to gain CSEC passes. When staff spoke with him about his experience they discovered that his academic difficulties did not necessarily reflect his ability.

“Sometimes all it takes is a change of environment for these youngsters, and at the Cadet Academy we’re thriving because, first and foremost, we have educators, we have our teachers, but love is central to what we do,” she said.

Johnson said that philosophy extends to how students are treated when they make mistakes. Rather than focusing on punishment, staff speak of corrective measures and ensure students have immediate access to adults when problems arise.

According to Johnson, the academy normally takes about 80 students in an intake and has approximately 10 resident facilitators and 15 external teachers, in addition to administrators, guidance counsellors, and access to the JCF’s medical services. It currently offers seven CSEC and four CAPE subjects.

The academy also serves as a potential pathway into the JCF, although Johnson stressed that becoming a cop is not compulsory and admission to the academy does not guarantee recruitment.

Students who want to join the force must still meet the requirements, sit the JCF entrance examination, and undergo further background checks.

Of the 35 students who graduated on June 25 this year, 34 were awaiting the next intake to join the JCF, while one planned to attend university first.

Johnson said that, overall, 99.9 per cent of students who choose to pursue policing after completing the programme progress towards the JCF, with more than 175 former cadets now serving in the organisation.

But the academy’s purpose is not simply to produce police personnel.

Johnson said students are encouraged to pursue tertiary education or other careers if that is the path they choose, while the JCF hopes the education and personal development they receive will prepare them for life beyond the academy.

The academy’s model comes against a separate national conversation about the performance of boys in Jamaica’s education system, where they continue to face challenges in areas such as engagement, attendance, and academic achievement.

That wider concern provides an important backdrop to the academy’s results, but Johnson said the programme itself grew from the JCF’s direct experience with young people and its decision to create a more concentrated intervention.

World.title: Kabaka Pyramid’s Rebel Music gets new life
World.content:
Kabaka Pyramid .

Fifteen years can change a lot in music. Trends come and go, audiences shift, and artistes inevitably evolve. But for Kabaka Pyramid, the years since his breakthrough Rebel Music EP have not meant abandoning the foundation on which his career was built. Instead, the Grammy Award-winning reggae artiste is returning to it.

On August 28, Kabaka will release Rebel Music – The Lyrics Tape, a 10-track project marking the 15th anniversary of the EP that helped introduce him to a wider audience and establish his reputation as one of Jamaica’s more lyrically conscious voices.

But the project is less about recreating 2011 and more about examining what has endured since then. Since his breakout year in music, he has moved from emerging artiste to international stages and even Grammy success with The Kalling.

Through it all, his ability to move between reggae, dancehall, and hip hop while maintaining an unmistakably Jamaican perspective has remained a defining feature of his music.

That musical identity is again at the centre of Rebel Music – The Lyrics Tape. Three songs already released from the project — Rotation, From Weh Day and We Dem Wah — offer a glimpse into the different influences that have shaped the artiste.

“There is so much going on in the world, and I really believe if we played more reggae we would be better off,” Kabaka Pyramid said. “Reggae has a healing nature. The music has always been able to uplift people, bring people together and give us something positive to hold on to.”

With that said, he is encouraging DJs, selectors, and veteran artistes to invest in younger talent, a plight that makes the anniversary project about more than Kabaka’s own journey.

Fifteen years after Rebel Music helped him find his audience, he is using that milestone to question whether emerging reggae acts are being given similar opportunities to find theirs.

Across its 10 tracks, the project moves through cultural commentary, reflection, reggae consciousness, dancehall energy, and lyrical competition. In doing so it connects the artiste he was becoming 15 years ago with the one he is today.

For an artiste, longevity is not simply measured by how long one manages to remain visible. Sometimes it is also measured by whether the things that mattered at the beginning still matter after the success arrives. Fifteen years later, Kabaka Pyramid appears to be making his answer clear: The music may evolve, but the foundation remains.

Rebel Music – The Lyrics Tape will be available on all major digital streaming platforms.

— Shereita Grizzle

World.title: HARD ROCK CLEARS CABINET HURDLE
World.content:
Hard Rock International has received Cabinet approval for a proposed integrated resort development in Montego Bay, but separate regulatory approval is required before casino gaming can begin..

HARD ROCK International has received Cabinet approval for a proposed integrated resort development in Montego Bay, clearing a key government hurdle for a planned hotel and casino within a wider three-phase development, with projected investment of US$756.9 million.

The approval was disclosed to the Jamaica Observer last Monday by a person familiar with the process who asked not to be identified because the decision had not yet been publicly announced.

Hard Rock subsequently confirmed the approval in written responses to Business Observer queries.

“Hard Rock International is pleased to confirm that we have been granted a provisional casino licence for an integrated resort in Montego Bay,” the company said on Friday.

“We are honoured by this opportunity and look forward to bringing our distinctive blend of world-class hospitality, entertainment, and exceptional guest experiences to Jamaica.”

Hard Rock did not identify the government authority that issued the approval, the legal entity that received it, or any conditions attached.

The approval moves the project forward but it does not by itself permit Hard Rock or an affiliated company to operate a casino in Jamaica.

Casino Gaming Commission Chief Executive Officer Cleveland Allen, responding to questions from the Business Observer, said Jamaica’s regulatory framework requires separate approvals for an integrated resort development and the operation of a casino.

At the first stage, a developer must secure approval from the minister responsible for finance through an Approved Integrated Resort Development (AIRD) Order under Section 9 of the Casino Gaming Act.

“The making of an AIRD Order does not, by itself, authorise casino gaming,” Allen said. “Rather, it establishes the developer’s eligibility to proceed to the second stage by applying to the Casino Gaming Commission for a casino gaming licence.”

Allen did not say whether an AIRD Order has been formally issued for the Hard Rock development or whether Hard Rock or an affiliated Jamaican company has applied to the commission for a casino gaming licence.

Jamaica allows casinos only as part of larger tourism developments offering hotel accommodation, entertainment, sporting facilities, and other visitor services.

Government filings place the proposed Hard Rock hotel and casino within a three-phase development on the same property in Montego Bay.

A table prepared by Jamaica Promotions Corporation (Jampro), and included in the Government of Jamaica’s annual report for the 2025/26 financial year, identifies UNICO Resort as the first phase of the Hard Rock Hotel development.

The 451-room UNICO is under construction. Work began in October 2023 and completion is expected by the end of 2026, according to the report. Jampro placed the projected capital expenditure at US$250.2 million and estimated that the development would generate 1,000 temporary and 1,000 permanent jobs.

The second phase, identified as Hard Rock Hotel – Phase 2 – RCD Hotel Group, is projected to have 1,100 rooms and require US$373.3 million in capital expenditure.

Jampro said land clearing and preliminary groundwork had started on that phase, which will be built on the same Montego Bay property adjacent to UNICO. It projected 1,300 temporary jobs during development and 1,200 permanent positions.

DOMA Residences, the third phase, is planned as a 250-room development valued at US$133.4 million. The government report said construction was estimated to begin in 2026 on the same property, beside UNICO and the Hard Rock hotel.

Together, the three phases account for a projected 1,801 rooms, US$756.9 million in capital expenditure, 3,300 temporary jobs and 3,200 permanent positions, based on the figures supplied to Jampro.

The government filing does not specify whether Cabinet’s integrated resort approval covers all three phases or only the proposed hotel and casino component.

Hard Rock International is owned by the Seminole Tribe of Florida, which acquired the brand in 2007. The company says its network comprises more than 300 hotels, casinos, cafes, entertainment venues and retail locations across more than 80 countries.

The process followed by Princess Grand Jamaica Resort in Green Island, Hanover, illustrates the distinction between approval of an integrated resort and the licensing of its casino.

Allen said an AIRD Order for the Princess Integrated Resort Development was issued in August 2023. The resort opened in December 2024, and an application for a casino gaming licence was submitted in August 2025.

The commission approved the application in July 2026 after completing its assessment and due diligence. It was the first casino operator’s licence granted under Jamaica’s regulatory framework.

The licence was issued to Adamas Grand Casino Limited, which will operate the proposed casino at Princess Grand under a management agreement with Grupo Orenes, a Spanish gaming and hospitality company.

The licence does not allow the casino to open immediately. Adamas must first meet the commission’s pre-operational requirements and receive clearance to begin operating.

World.title: ‘RAIN DELAY’ FOR JCA AGM
World.content:
A view of Sabina Park, headquarters of the Jamaica Cricket Association, during a rain delay in a West Indies versus Sri Lanka One-Day International game in June.garfield Robinson

JAMAICA Cricket Association (JCA) President Dr Donovan Bennett says the voting annual general meeting (AGM) is likely to be held in October, after it was previously postponed.

The JCA annual meeting and election were to have been held in May but were pushed back pending ratification of proposed governance changes to its constitution.

Bennett told the Jamaica Observer that the board will get the opportunity to ratify the changes in just over two weeks.

“We will have a special meeting in September to deal with matters that we have had hanging around for years. Immediately after that September 10 meeting we will set a date for the AGM. I imagine that we will have the voting AGM in October,” he said.

Bennett, who had previously served as JCA vice-president, swept to power in April 2024 when he defeated the incumbent President Wilford “Billy” Heaven.

He admitted that, ideally, he had wanted the elections to be held months ago, but those plans had to be put aside.

“I would have preferred to have had the AGM exactly after two years — which would have been about March/April — but it didn’t happen.

“The AGM is not constitutionally due until December but… we don’t want to take it down to the last,” he said.

Though choosing to not outline granular details, Bennett insisted the constitutional changes are important for the greater good of cricket in Jamaica.

“It’s a matter of our constitution and [about] what we have and what we need to have,” he said, noting there are current glaring governance loopholes in how the JCA can regulate clubs and parish associations.

The JCA president said he is eager to be given a fresh mandate in his bid to improve the struggling sport in the country, and by extension the region.

“I get the impression there are some positive movements in the game, so I’m just hoping we can accelerate that process because we really want to get back to the top as soon as possible. It’s very important for West Indies cricket that Jamaica does well. Jamaica has the largest economy and the largest population so it stands to reason that if Jamaica does well then West indies cricket will do well,” he argued.

While Bennett is likely to return to the top post unopposed, there is intrigue surrounding the first vice-president job. Both the incumbent Fritz Harris, the Clarendon Cricket Association president, and Nehemiah Perry, former West Indies off spinner and current head of Kingston Cricket Club, were previously nominated.

However, Bennett confirmed that the nomination process will be redone ahead of the rescheduled elections.

— Sanjay Myers

World.title: Atlantic Hardware turns to e-commerce as profit triples
World.content:
For both its three-month an half-year results, Atlantic posted record revenues and profits.

ATLANTIC Hardware & Plumbing Company Limited is preparing to introduce e-commerce and expand its product portfolio after revenue jumped 69 per cent and profit more than tripled during the first half of 2026.

Managing Director Deanall Barnes told the Jamaica Observer on Monday that the hardware distributor had begun discussions on establishing an e-commerce platform as part of a wider effort to strengthen its digital footprint and use technology to improve its operations.

“On the technology front, we have commenced discussions on introducing an e-commerce platform, alongside broader consideration of how technology can be used to enhance the business — from inventory management to customer service — ultimately with a view of continuing to improve our bottom line,” he said to the Business Observer.

The digital push follows a sharp increase in sales at the company, which listed on the Junior Market of the Jamaica Stock Exchange in April 2025.

For the three months ended June 30, Atlantic reported record revenue of $776.4 million, up 92 per cent from $404.8 million in the corresponding quarter last year. Net profit rose 140 per cent to $42 million from $17.5 million.

Revenue for the six-month period increased 69 per cent year-on-year to $1.46 billion, while net profit more than tripled to $116.3 million from $33.9 million.

The company’s balance sheet also strengthened, as shareholders’ equity rose to $596.3 million and cash and cash equivalents more than doubled year-on-year to $255 million. Total assets on the other hand stood at $1.6 billion at the end of June.

Atlantic, which has operated since 1994 and distributes more than 2,400 hardware and building products from leading global brands, including Stanley, DeWalt, Black & Decker, Bosch and WD-40.

For its 2025 financial year, the company recorded revenue of $1.8 billion and net profit of $68.9 million.

Barnes said Atlantic’s new agricultural distribution division had become a significant contributor to revenue and was expected to support further growth as the company added products.

Launched earlier this year, the division has distribution rights for brands, including Bonanza seeds, Nutramix feed, and Bellota machetes. It generated approximately $300 million in revenue during the first half of 2026.

“We continue to expand within that category and will shortly be introducing a wider variety of seeds and pesticides — these products have already been tested by our suppliers, orders have been placed, and we anticipate arrival by mid-third quarter,” Barnes said.

He said Atlantic also sees opportunities to expand the division into fertilisers, veterinary products, and home and garden lines while assessing other categories that complement its existing distribution infrastructure and broad customer base.

As the company adjusts its procurement strategy in response to disruptions to global shipping, Barnes said it continues to deepen relationships with local and regional suppliers to reduce the risk of stock-outs as it manages its expanded portfolio.

The strategy has become increasingly important as Atlantic continues to widen its product offerings while seeking to maintain reliable supplies for customers.

Despite potentially subdued macroeconomic conditions, Barnes said management remains cautiously optimistic about the company’s prospects for the remainder of the financial year.

As the company plans to continue growing market share by widening its range of traditional hardware and building products alongside increasing its participation in government projects, the managing director said it will also tighten partnerships with suppliers to target major hotel developments.

“Disciplined capital allocation and continued balance sheet strength remain central to funding this growth,” Barnes said.

World.title: ‘Baddies build furniture too’
World.content:
Carpenter Sydonie Miller at her shop in DunKirk, Kingston (Photo: Garfield Robinson).

With work hard to find and financial constraints mounting during the coronavirus pandemic, one Jamaican woman discovered a hidden talent that opened an unexpected livelihood for her in a labour-intensive trade not often pursued by local females – carpentry.

Twenty-nine-year-old Sydonie Miller had been finding it difficult to secure a job in 2020, during the heights of COVID-19, despite having a bachelor’s degree in business management and secretarial skills.

Miller, who was a new mother at the time, said her husband, a taxi operator, was the only one working and she was determined to find a way to contribute to her family.

Her journey to carpentry began with a desire to own a padded bedhead and being quoted what she considered an exorbitant price to have one made.

“At the time, it was padded bed did run the place. When I go to ask the price, them a give me an arm and a leg for it. Me say me nah pay that,” Miller told Observer Online.

So, she decided to build it herself.

Seeking the guidance of a carpenter friend on Charles Street and gathering the necessary materials, Miller went on to make her first bedhead.

After completing the project, Miller’s curiosity and determination pushed her to learn more. She eventually made her way to Oxford Street, where veteran carpenters such as Chucky, Paul, Max, Abi Doll and Warren took her under their wings and taught her how to build a wider range of furniture, including dressers, chests of drawers and beds.

But for Miller, learning the trade was not difficult because she has always been a practical learner. She quickly grasped the skills being taught to her.

“If you’re going to do something, I see what you’re doing. If you show me one time, you don’t have to show me again. Just the one time, I know what to do,” she explained.

But the mother of three said her entry into carpentry was about more than simply learning how to build furniture. She believes the skill was placed in her path for a reason.

“At the time, I was at work and I can’t forget the day. The almighty say I give you a skill, go and use it. I have business management, secretarial skills. I thought it was that skill but I never knew it was this skill. So when him say I give you a skill, go and use it, me just say alright me ago just go deal with the bed head. Me see say me can build dresser and me just a build. Me go under the wings of the veterans,” she said.

Miller, who now owns her very own furniture business, Luxurious Furnitures by Syd, said her client base now ranges from individual customers to stores in the downtown Kingston area.

When Observer Online visited her shop on Banana Street in the McIntyre Villa community of East Kingston, Miller was seen working on a bedhead and bed bottom for one of her customers.

While her skills have helped her build a business, Miller said being a woman in a male-dominated trade has presented its own challenges.

“Some of them, when them see a woman come and say you know say me build this, them don’t believe it” she explained.

Miller said some customers only become convinced that she builds the furniture herself after seeing a male carpenter deliver one of her pieces.

Despite the doubters, Miller said she has also encountered customers who appreciate the fact that she is a woman in the trade and are willing to give her the time needed to complete their furniture.

“To be honest, it’s a bittersweet moment, but at the end of the day there are some people that really love me, who are really happy that I’m a woman and I do this. You have some patient ones, big up on unu self. Them say alright then, I’ll give you time,” she added.

The carpenter said each piece of furniture requires patience and attention to detail, with the process involving several stages before a finished product is ready.

“For me its patience, to really put in the work, because remember, furniture building takes time. It has different layers, different processes to build. So to build a bed head like this, it takes time. I have a lot of different grades of sanding to do,” she said.

She further explained: “I have to start the sanding from, like, 80, and I go down to 180. Then I go down to 200. Then I go down to 220. It’s patience. And you have to get all the nooks and crannies. You can’t just sand off just the bigger parts. You have to sand from the corners, from underneath, behind, everything. So it’s just patience.”

Of all the furniture she has made since entering the trade, Miller said one particular piece remains her favourite, a king-size mahogany bed set. She said the piece holds special significance because it challenged her skills when she was still new to furniture building.

Miller is now encouraging other women not to allow traditional perceptions about certain professions to prevent them from pursuing their interests.

“Don’t follow the stigma say a man work. Woman can do it, too. Once you see something that you want to do just do it. Learn the skill, do it, because at the end of the day, it’s not who do it. It’s really how you set your mind to do it or if you have the determination to do it,” Miller said. “So don’t follow them a man work. Baddies build furniture too. Baddies build furniture too.”

World.title: Fewer students drunk or high
World.content:
(Photo: Adobe stock)

THE National Council on Drug Abuse (NCDA) is reporting that fewer teenagers are using illegal drugs or drinking alcohol across Jamaica, but the numbers remain concerning.

According to the NCDA, its recent Global School-Based Health Survey (GSHS) conducted January to March 2026 — which had 3,058 respondents from 32 schools, with 76 per cent participation among students and 100 per cent from schools — showed that the consumption of alcohol by students in grades seven to 11 dropped from 52.5 per cent in 2010 to 38.8 per cent in 2026.

At the same time, the number of children who started consumption of alcohol before age 14 has decreased from 80.2 per cent in 2010 to 71.5 per cent this year. Also, teenagers who get drunk after the consumption of alcoholic beverages dropped from 35.5 per cent in 2010 to 21.5 per cent in 2026.

But 10.3 per cent of adolescents still attend school under the influence of alcohol, and 10.6 per cent are exposed to s about alcohol.

The NCDA — an agency of the Ministry of Health and Wellness — believes the overall message for positive trends has been working; however, it says continued action is needed to strengthen early prevention programmes, enforce underage drinking laws, reduce youth exposure to alcohol marketing, and increase parent and school engagements.

The survey also found that the use of ganja among adolescents declined from 21.5 per cent in 2017 to 15.7 per cent in 2026, a trend welcomed by the NCDA.

However, the organisation says it is concerned that 24.3 per cent of adolescents have easy access to the weed, while it noticed an emergence in the use of ecstasy, also known as molly.

Ecstasy is a synthetic psychoactive drug with both stimulant and psychedelic effects. Teens use it at parties and other gatherings, but it can cause dangerous spikes in body temperature, dehydration, high blood pressure, and heart failure.

With some students still attending school under the influence of substances because of the easy access to ganja and ecstasy, the NCDA says it will be expanding its substance-use prevention programme, aimed at strengthening prevention, delaying initiation, reducing access, and providing timely support for young people.

It also plans to improve the monitoring of emerging drugs.

In the meantime, the GSHS found that physical fights among students declined from 50.1 per cent in 2010 to 27 per cent in 2026, while injuries from fights dropped from 59.6 per cent in 2010 to 49 per cent in 2026.

In addition, the survey says bullying dropped from 40.2 per cent in 2016 to 27 per cent in 2026.

However, the survey found that 15 per cent of teenagers faced cyber bullying in the past year but there was no comparative figure with 2010. Another 16.9 per cent experienced bullying off school compounds.

The NCDA said despite a drop in physical fights among students, it will be strengthening its violence-prevention programme as it seeks to maintain safe school policies.

“Safe environments are essential for academic success and healthy development,” said the NCDA.

“Violence and injuries impact students’ physical and mental health, learning and well-being. Bullying and cyberbullying can lead to anxiety, depression, low self-esteem, and social isolation,” the NCDA added.

The GSHS is an international gold-standard survey developed by World Health Organization, in collaboration with United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF); United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO); United States Agency for International Development (USAID), and the United States-based Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

It measures health behaviours and protective factors among students 13 to 17 years of age and is used in 110 countries.

World.title: Metsola praises Meloni’s ‘common-sense solutions’ on EU simplification
World.content:
The speech at the annual Meeting Rimini festival comes as Metsola seeks a third term at the helm of Parliament, potentially positioning her for a bid for the European Commission presidency in 2029. A Maltese national fluent in Italian, she regularly travels to Italy and meets officials in Rome, fueling speculation that she is working to build Italian support for 2029.

Metsola took a stab at the EU’s own landmark packaging regulation, which passed during her last mandate — a law Italy has lobbied against in Brussels.

The rules “impose rigid and counterproductive burdens on European small and medium-sized enterprises,” which is "the exact opposite of what Europe should represent," Metsola said.

Since the law came into force this month, companies have been required to cover the costs of managing the packaging they place on the market once it becomes waste — a system known as extended producer responsibility. They must also appoint a representative in every EU country where they sell their products. The European Commission suggested scrapping that requirement in December to make compliance easier. EU governments oppose the idea, while some MEPs want to drop the measure for small and medium-sized companies only.

“I am proud that the European Parliament has taken the initiative to correct this situation in the coming weeks,” said Metsola.

The MEPs' work on this file is ongoing and the Parliament isn’t expected to vote on the proposal until October, when lawmakers will negotiate a final version of the text with EU countries.

Die Forderung nach millionenfacher „Remigration“ prägt die Politik der AfD. Migrationsforscher Gerald Knaus erklärt im Gespräch mit Pauline von Pezold und Frederik Schindler, warum diese Pläne eklatant gegen die Menschenwürde verstoßen. Die Partei nutze dabei nach außen gezielt eine verharmlosende Doppelmoral.

Knaus warnt eindringlich vor den internationalen Vorbildern der Partei, etwa den massenhaften Deportationsplänen aus dem Umfeld von Donald Trump. Die völkische Sprache von Politikern wie Björn Höcke erinnere zudem stark an die NPD und die fatalen Jugoslawienkriege der 90er-Jahre.

Um ihre extremen Pläne rechtlich überhaupt umsetzen zu können, müsste Deutschland laut Knaus aus der EU und sämtlichen Menschenrechtsabkommen austreten. Die AfD nehme den völligen Zusammenbruch des Systems der Bundesrepublik dafür ganz bewusst in Kauf.

Gerald Knaus war 2016 Mitinitiator und -aushandler des Flüchtlingspakts zwischen der Türkei und der EU. Er ist Mitgründer und Vorsitzender der Denkfabrik Europäische Stabilitätsinitiative. Im vergangenen Jahr ist sein Buch „Welches Europa brauchen wir? Ein politisches Wunder und wie wir es vor seinen Feinden schützen“ erschienen.

Das Buch “Höcke – Ein Rechtsextremist auf dem Weg zur Macht. Die AfD und ihr gefährlichster Vordenker“ ist im Verlag Herder erschienen.

„Inside AfD“ ist der POLITICO-Podcast über die umstrittenste Partei des Landes. Trotz Radikalisierung und Beobachtung durch den Verfassungsschutz wächst die AfD weiter. Wie ist das möglich?
