World.title: Canada’s Carney to attend EU’s State of the Union
World.content:
European Commission President Ursula Von der Leyen speaks with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney during the G7 Summit in Kananaskis on June 16, 2025. | Pool photo by Ludovic Marin/AFP via Getty Images

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney will join European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen for the most high-profile political moment in the EU's calendar, amid a worsening rift between the U.S. and Ottawa.

A European Commission official close to von der Leyen confirmed to POLITICO that Carney had accepted an invitation to attend the State of the EU speech in Strasbourg on Sept. 16, where the president will set out her priorities for the bloc.

"Before the summer break, the European Commission President invited Prime Minister Carney for [the State of the Union] both as a strong sign of the closeness of the EU and Canada, and to clearly signal the intention and ambition on both sides to upgrade our partnership," the official said. "In these challenging times, strengthening our relationships across the world is vital."

World.title: Musk to receive Ukraine’s Order of Freedom from Zelenskyy
World.content:
Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite internet service has helped Ukrainian forces maintain communications and coordinate operations since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022. | Imen Ben Youssef/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images

The honor comes as Kyiv tries to persuade the tech mogul to let its army use Starlink inside Russian territory.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has awarded his country’s Order of Freedom to Elon Musk Wednesday, amid efforts to persuade Musk to expand access to his Starlink network.

Zelenskyy’s presidential decree praises Musk for “protecting people’s lives and freedom, and developing relations between the peoples of Ukraine and the United States of America.”

Musk’s Starlink satellite internet service has helped Ukrainian forces maintain communications and coordinate operations since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022. In February 2026, SpaceX disabled thousands of Starlink terminals used by Russian forces, weakening their military capabilities.

Ukraine is trying to convince the tech mogul to allow its army to use the Starlink network within Russian territory. Doing so would allow Ukraine to improve the accuracy of missile and drone strikes deep inside Russia. “For now, Musk has said that this would be an escalation. But he may change his mind when he sees more arguments,” Zelenskyy told journalists last Saturday.

The Order of Freedom is often awarded to foreign leaders for their support for Ukraine — recent recipients include French President Emmanuel Macron, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda.

World.title: France and Germany collide over Europe’s industrial future
World.content:
France and Germany are clashing over how far the EU should go to protect European industry — with Paris pushing stronger “Made in Europe” rules and Berlin warning against provoking new trade fights.

Zoya Sheftalovich and Ian Wishart look at what that battle says about Europe’s struggle to go green, stay competitive and keep its markets open at the same time.

Then, Brussels is rattled by another wave of shootings. We look at the drug trade behind much of the violence, the Antwerp connection, and the political fight over whether the capital has enough police resources — or whether Belgium’s fragmented system is part of the problem.

And on a much lighter note: Eurostar may finally get some serious competition. New operators are lining up to run through the Channel Tunnel, raising the prospect of more trains — and maybe cheaper tickets — between Brussels and London.

World.title: Kemi Badenoch’s Conservatives wish they could be as popular as she is
World.content:
“Kemi is popular. We are trying to promote the rest of the shadow Cabinet to make sure that popularity rubs off on the rest of the party,” said one Badenoch staffer, granted anonymity because they were not authorized to speak on the record.

So far, it hasn’t worked.

“Badenoch’s success has still failed to translate into any meaningful movement in the polls for her party,” said Scarlett Maguire, founder of independent polling firm Merlin Strategy. “The Conservatives’ mediocre polling numbers, still worse than when they lost the 2024 election, shows the extent to which they have lost trust in their brand.”

New look conference

The party’s first big set piece moment this autumn will come when the Conservative Party meets for its annual conference in Birmingham at the beginning of October.

Badenoch’s performance at last year’s gathering marked the beginning of her transformation as party leader, and her team is hoping to repeat the trick by making this year’s conference more Badenoch-focused.

There will be less policy this year, according to one shadow minister familiar with the plans and also granted anonymity to speak freely.

World.title: Comment “le mur de fer” promis contre l’immigration clandestine à Mayotte s’est enlisé
World.content:
Un plan opérationnel “avant fin 2029, voire 2030”

Un appel d’offres, publié par le ministère de l’Intérieur le 12 août et repéré par POLITICO, dévoile l’ampleur du retard pris par le programme “mur de fer”. Celui-ci vise à recruter un prestataire extérieur, dont le rôle sera justement d’accompagner l’administration dans la mise en place globale du dispositif. Selon le phasage détaillé dans le règlement de consultation de l’appel d’offres, le plan “Uhura wa shaba”, dans toutes ses composantes, pourrait ne pas être pleinement opérationnel avant fin 2029, voire 2030.

En effet, une fois le prestataire sélectionné — fin 2026, au plus tôt, d’après les délais fixés dans ce document — celui-ci devra s’engager dans la préparation, puis l’organisation d’un “dialogue compétitif” pour choisir les industriels susceptibles de fournir les équipements et technologies nécessaires, pour une période de 33 mois au total. S’en suivra la phase “d’exécution” de ce chantier, pendant 51 mois.

“Si l’on fait les comptes, cela renvoie la mise en place du rideau de fer à 2030-2034, ce n’est pas acceptable”, s’agace Saïd Omar Oili. “J’y vois le signe que le gouvernement veut sous-traiter au privé la réflexion globale de la lutte contre l’immigration à Mayotte, un sujet de souveraineté, fustige Estelle Youssouffa. Lancer un tel chantier maintenant, c’est aussi un constat d’échec sur ce qui a été fait ces dernières années”.

Les radars actuels moins performants que les précédents

Dans l’appel d’offres, le ministère reconnaît lui-même que la “couverture des radars installés au début des années 2000 est significativement incomplète”. Celle-ci s’est retrouvée d’autant plus fragilisée par la tempête Chido qui a détruit une large partie des moyens de surveillance et d’interception.

“Des mesures de rattrapage ont été déployées : quatre radars légers et des caméras longue portée ont été achetés”, affirme le ministère de l’Intérieur, sollicité par POLITICO. Mais “ces radars ne disposent toutefois pas d’une portée de détection équivalente à celle des anciens radars”, pointe un rapport sénatorial publié en avril 2026 sur Mayotte et la Réunion. Le programme “rideau de fer […] n’a pas tenu ses promesses”, conclut ce document.

Selon les projections inscrites dans le marché public, le rideau de fer devait rendre “atteignable” l’interpellation de 20 000 étrangers en situation irrégulière en mer par an, contre 4 584 en 2025, d’après le bilan de la préfecture de Mayotte. Cette année-là, un total de 23 421 personnes ont fait l’objet d’un éloignement du territoire.

World.title: Spain cuts estimate of minors in Ceuta after duplicates found in database
World.content:
Spanish police have revised down the number of minors recorded in Ceuta following the mass arrival of migrants from Morocco last month, after discovering duplicate entries in their databases.

 

According to the Interior Ministry, some procedures involving the same child had been recorded as separate cases, inflating the overall figure.

On 18 August, police said they had located, identified and placed 2,168 minors in the care of the Ceuta authorities since the mass arrival of people from Morocco on 30 July and up to 09:00 that morning. Following a review of the records, the figure now stands at around 1,500.

The total also includes minors who were already in the care of Ceuta's child protection services before 30 July. The Interior Ministry said the number could rise as ongoing identification procedures are completed.

For now, the minors remain in Ceuta while authorities consider options including transferring them to other Spanish regions because the city does not have sufficient reception capacity or, in some cases, returning them to their countries of origin.

Among them are children and teenagers from countries including Chad and Sudan, both affected by conflict and humanitarian crises. Save the Children has said some may be entitled to international protection.

The organisation has also highlighted the particular vulnerability of women and girls, who may face risks including forced marriage, sexual violence and trafficking.

Government to discuss transfers with regions

Spain's central government has called a meeting with the country's autonomous regions on Thursday to discuss transferring minors from territories where reception systems, including Ceuta's, are under pressure.

The meeting will also discuss the transfer of €25 million to Ceuta to strengthen its capacity to care for minors.

Regional governments controlled by the conservative Popular Party have opposed the government's proposed distribution system. The coalition governments of Aragon, Extremadura and Castile and León, where the far-right Vox party is responsible for children's services, have said they will not attend the meeting.

Another option is to return some minors to their countries of origin, although this is subject to strict legal safeguards.

Returns can take place only after an individual assessment determines that it is in the child's best interests. In practice, such returns are rare.

Spain's Supreme Court has previously ruled that the mass return to Morocco of unaccompanied minors following the 2021 migration crisis was unlawful.

The court found that safeguards required under Spanish immigration law had been ignored, including the obligation to examine each child's individual circumstances.

Those safeguards must be respected even when a bilateral agreement exists, such as the 2007 deal between Spain and Morocco intended to facilitate the coordinated return of minors. The Spanish government cited that agreement when seeking to justify the 2021 returns.

World.title: Can flying taxis beat LA traffic? US city to develop air taxi vertiport ahead of 2028 Olympics
World.content:
It doesn’t quite feel like two years have passed since the Paris Olympics drew to a close. But with Los Angeles now gearing up to welcome the world in 2028, fans planning a trip to the next Games just might have a very LA way of avoiding one of the city’s most notorious problems: traffic – and lots of it.

 

The Californian city is set to develop its first “vertiport”, which is a dedicated takeoff and landing site for electric air taxis. Spearheaded by sports entertainment giant AEG and Archer Aviation, the site will be hosted in L.A. Live, a four-million-square-foot sports and entertainment district in downtown Los Angeles.

And for visitors faced with navigating one of the world’s busiest cities during one of the world’s biggest sporting events, the appeal is obvious: fly over the traffic rather than… just sit in it.

Archer’s Midnight aircraft has a fully-electric system and can seat up to four passengers. With a top speed of 241.4 kilometres/hour, it also gets them where they need to go quicker than driving.

The company says an air taxi flight from Hawthorne Airport to Orange County, famed for cruises out of Newport Harbor for dolphin and whale watching, takes around 12 minutes. In comparison, it would take about a 56-minute car ride.

Meanwhile, a flight from Hollywood Burbank Airport to Inglewood’s SoFi Stadium takes 14 minutes, compared to an almost hour-long journey on wheels.

This will be especially useful come 2028. In the run up to the LA Games, SoFi has now been dubbed “2028 Stadium”, and is set to become the largest swimming venue in Olympic history. It will also co-host the Olympics opening ceremony, alongside the LA Memorial Coliseum as well as host the Paralympics opening ceremony.

Last year, Archer Aviation was handpicked as the Official Air Taxi Provider of the LA28 Games and Team USA. To celebrate this, Archer unveiled its Team USA livery with a display of its Midnight aircraft at L.A Live.

World.title: UK PM Burnham planning US visit in September to push further support for Ukraine
World.content:
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham is planning a visit to New York in September, where he is expected to press US President Donald Trump for further support for Ukraine.

 

World leaders are scheduled to meet in the city next month for the United Nations General Assembly, with military aid for Kyiv set to be high on the agenda.

In an interview with Bloomberg earlier this week, Burnham said he was "looking forward to going to New York in September."

"I've not fully confirmed the details yet, but it's likely I will go, particularly after today's discussion," he told the outlet, referencing talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. "Leaving today, I'm quite clear what I need to do in the next few weeks".

If confirmed, it would mark Burnham's first official visit to the US since he took over as prime minister in July.

The prime minister's comments come amid continued calls from Zelenskyy for more interceptor missiles, particularly US-made Patriots, to defend against increasing Russian ballistic missile attacks.

Speaking to Bloomberg, Burnham said he believed the issue of Ukraine's dwindling interceptor stockpiles was "fixable" but that any solution would likely require "a lot of layers and a lot of negotiation."

Burnham was in Kyiv on Monday as western leaders took part in events marking Ukraine's Independence Day.

In a speech delivered from the capital, he reiterated his support for Ukraine in spite of what he called Russia's "outrageous threats" against the UK. The Russian Embassy in London had earlier this month threatened "consequences" after accusing Britain of "deliberately opting for an escalation of the Ukraine crisis."

"We are with you in this struggle all the way heart and soul," Burnham said. "And as prime minister, let me say that I am with you personally".

The UK also announced this week that it would be providing Ukraine with the technology to produce its own Storm Shadow cruise missiles as it ramps up its support for the country.

Luke Pollard, the UK's Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, said the move would create "more deterrence against Russian aggression."

Patriot missiles

Zelenskyy's main wish, however, is the US' coveted Patriot missiles.

The Patriot system is one of the most advanced air defence systems in the world and, while costly, can be used to defend against a range of hostile targets, including ballistic and cruise missiles, aircraft, and loitering munitions.

A Patriot missile mobile launcher is displayed outside the Fort Sill Army Post near Lawton, Okla., on March 21, 2023. Copyright 2023 The Associated Press. All rights reserved.

In July, Trump seemingly agreed to provide Kyiv with a license to produce missiles for the system domestically, but he later backtracked, saying you have to be "very careful about letting somebody build them."

In a post on X on Sunday, Zelenskyy said he "wanted to secure 300 missiles for the Patriot systems" as part of a winter package.

"I would very much like to believe that we can find a way to access some small percentage of U.S. stockpiles – say, 5% or 10%. And we are ready to pay for those supplies," he wrote.

World.title: Belgian fries under threat as potatoes shrink in heat
World.content:
Belgian potato farmers are warning that this year's crop could be too small to make the country's famous fries after extreme weather hit harvests.

 

In Amay, near the eastern city of Liège, farmer Mathieu Comijn is pulling Bintje potatoes from parched soil that are barely the size of ping-pong balls.

“You can see the soil is extremely dry,” Comijn said. “Normally, they should be at least four times this size. At the moment we can't make fries with these potatoes.”

Heavy rain and storms at the end of spring weakened the soil before exceptionally hot and dry summer weather prevented the potatoes from developing normally.

The Comijn family grows around 500 hectares of potatoes and has contracts requiring it to deliver agreed volumes to processors. It plans to draw on stocks from last year's unusually abundant harvest to meet some of those commitments.

Belgium is the world's biggest exporter of frozen fries, with its potato-processing industry handling more than six million tonnes annually. Around 90% of the frozen fries it produces are exported to more than 120 markets.

The shortage could eventually feed through to consumers.

At Brussels' well-known Maison Antoine fry kiosk, owner Pascal Willaert explains that large, elongated potatoes were ideal for making fries.

“But right now, with the seasons varying so wildly, it's hard to find the perfect potato for fries,” he said.

Belgium's national association of fry vendors, representing around 4,500 shops, has also warned that tighter potato supplies could push prices higher.

World.title: What message did the CIA director deliver to Moscow — on Ukraine, NATO or Iran?
World.content:
CIA Director John Ratcliffe’s surprise visit to Moscow on Tuesday sparked speculation about the trip's sudden nature and what message Washington considered important enough for the US spy chief to deliver in person.

 

The Kremlin confirmed that Ratcliffe held talks with Russian intelligence officials during his hours-long visit, but said he did not meet Vladimir Putin.

“No meetings with Putin were planned,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said.

Putin was briefed on the outcome of the discussions, according to the Kremlin.

Neither Washington nor Moscow have disclosed what was discussed, leaving the purpose of the unusual visit unclear.

Ratcliffe travelled to the Russian capital on Tuesday in his first known visit to Russia since becoming CIA director, making the journey at a particularly tense moment in Moscow's all-out war in Ukraine and amid growing concern over possible Russian escalation against Europe.

But its timing, the precautions surrounding Ratcliffe's arrival and his position within the Trump administration prompted speculation that the CIA director was carrying a message considerably more sensitive than those normally handled through diplomatic channels.

The US asked Ukraine not to strike Moscow or St Petersburg while Ratcliffe was in Russia, according to reports citing people familiar with the matter.

Kyiv reportedly learned that a senior US delegation would travel to Russia, but was not initially told that Ratcliffe would be part of it.

The request is significant given Ukraine's expanding campaign of long-range strikes inside Russia, including attacks against energy and military infrastructure as well as sites financing the Russian war machine.

FILE - Smoke rises following a Ukrainian drone attack on a warehouse for online retailer Wildberries in St. Petersburg, Russia on Friday, July 24, 2026 AP photo

A warning to Moscow?

One possibility is that Ratcliffe travelled to Moscow to warn of the risk of further Russian escalation.

US intelligence reportedly raised concerns that Moscow could be preparing for further mobilisation not only to sustain its war against Ukraine but also to seek to test NATO's resolve through provocations against alliance members.

The visit comes amid growing concern over Russian activity in NATO territory, following a series of suspected sabotage operations and drone incursions in recent months.

The theory draws a striking parallel with the last known visit to Moscow by a CIA director.

William Burns travelled to the Russian capital in November 2021, as Russian forces were massing around Ukraine, to warn the Kremlin against an invasion and spell out the consequences Washington believed would follow.

Despite repeated assurances from Moscow that it had no plans to invade Ukraine, Russia launched its full-scale invasion three months later.

Ratcliffe is also regarded as one of the senior Trump administration officials most supportive of continued US assistance to Ukraine, including intelligence used to support Kyiv's long-range operations.

His arrival therefore came at a sensitive moment for both Moscow and Kyiv.

Donald Trump shakes hands John Ratcliffe as they speak with reporters in the James Brady Press Briefing Room at the White House, April 6, 2026, in Washington AP Photo

Ukraine, NATO or Iran?

Ukraine is not the only possible explanation.

The visit also comes amid mounting tensions between Washington and Moscow over Iran, Russia's closest partner in the Middle East.

Russia has been accused of providing Tehran with intelligence on US military assets, while Washington has stepped up economic pressure on Iran in a bid to finish the war it started in late February.

Peskov described contacts between the two intelligence services as positive but said it was too early to judge whether they could improve wider relations between Washington and Moscow.

Ratcliffe's visit was sensitive enough to remain unannounced and important enough for the CIA director to travel to Moscow himself, even if only for a few hours.

World.title: Canada wants to get closer to the EU - but how far can it go without EU membership?
World.content:
With the trade war with the US heating back up, Canada’s Prime minister Mark Carney has delivered another pledge to deepen his country's economic and security partnership with the EU.

 

His statement came after trade talks between Ottawa and Washington collapsed last week, with Canada accusing the US of interfering in its sovereignty by demanding French-language concessions.

In retaliation, US President Donald Trump said on Truth Social that on 1 January 2027, tariffs on cars and trucks will be increased to 50%.

“WE DON’T NEED CANADA, THEY NEED US!" he wrote. "They do 95% of their business with the US, with us, the exact opposite!”

Canada announced later that, as of 8 September, it would enact tariffs ranging from 15% to 50% on over 700 American imports, worth about $20 billion (€17.2 billion).

Since Trump’s return to power in 2025 and his repeated attacks on US-Canada trade relations, Ottawa has been turning several times towards the EU, seeking a stable relationship with a “like-minded” partner.

"This fall we will begin intense discussions with the European Union, the world's second-largest economy, to build a much stronger and deeper economic and security partnership,” Carney said on Monday.

The Canadian Prime minister has confirmed, according to Politico, that he will attend the State of the EU speech in Strasbourg on 16 September after European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen invited him before the trade war with the US broke out.

Since the start of the second Trump administration, Brussels and Ottawa have shared a common objective: diversifying their trade relations away from Washington. But since the EU and Canada are already bound by a trade agreement, how far could a deeper relationship go?

The truth is that both sides have their limits.

Intertwined Canadian and US markets

From critical raw materials to energy and defence, the last months have seen multiple areas of interest come to the fore, and they will likely set the agenda at the Canada-EU summit this fall.

Canada is planning to offer the EU better access to its critical raw materials. Brussels is desperate to move away from China, which holds the monopoly on the production and processing of rare earths. With strong domestic supplies of lithium, graphite and nickel, Ottawa has a lot to offer to integrate the EU into its metal value chain.

Canada might also make offers on energy, which it currently supplies principally to the US.

“We should be talking about a more viable Canada-EU corridor for energy, and not just in respect of oil and gas, but also of nuclear,” Mark Camilleri, President of the Canada-EU Trade and Investment Association, told Euronews. “The EU’s energy needs are increasing, and its energy supply is still very dependent on imports.”

On defence, Canada is already part of SAFE, the €150 billion defence instrument that supports EU member states that wish to invest in defence industrial production through common procurement. But defence cooperation is already set to go further, with Canada selecting German-Norwegian TKMS to build a new fleet of 12 submarines. Deepening the relationship on Arctic security could be another area of collaboration.

Canadian business, meanwhile, is increasingly interested in the European market, but the diversification will not come overnight. Geography, after all, matters.

“The Canadian economy is very much oriented and integrated to the US and North American economy,” Camilleri added. “We are not looking to untangle the relationship, despite the very distressing political issues taking place.”

The Europeans will also put limits on integration with Canada. The trade agreement struck in 2016 is proof enough that the EU market is not easy to access: the deal has not yet been ratified by all EU member states, and has only been provisionally applied since 2017.

Faint EU membership hopes

Geography matters not only for the Canadians, but also for the EU.

Article 49 of the Treaty on European Union opens membership to “any European State”. Morocco was not considered European enough in the past to become a member, so how could Canada, located much further away, be considered a “European state”?

Guntram Wolff, senior fellow at the Brussels-based think tank Bruegel, points out that there is a new openness in Brussels, and that a strategic alignment “could go far”, even if probably it has to fall short of full membership.

Liberalising trade further than what the current agreement involves could be an option. But how far could the integration of the Canadian market into the EU go?

“One can go to the point where Norway is, which is a single market membership,” Wolff told Euronews. “Whether that is where Canada wants to go and whether that's where all the European countries want to go, we will see in the coming weeks.”

Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein are members with EU member states of what is called the “European Economic Area”, membership of which involves the implementation of the EU's four freedoms – free movement of goods, persons, services and capital. These freedoms form the basis of the single market.

But an EU official told Euronews that this option was not on the table yet, and remains a theoretical debate for now.

World.title: Meta settles in US states lawsuit on teen user addiction
World.content:
Meta has agreed to pay what could amount to billions of dollars and to implement platform usage limitations on young users in a lawsuit brought by US states. The challenge revolved around addiction issues and overuse.

Meta, the parent company of Facebook and Instagram, has agreed to pay as much as $16.7 billion and to impose new limits on how teenagers use its social media sites as part of a lawsuit in California brought by a number of US states.

The settlement still requires court approval.

World.title: Reports: UEFA backs off FIFA boycott threat
World.content:
UEFA is reportedly set to withdraw a threat to boycott FIFA tournaments over a plan to partially privatize football tournaments. The Under-20 Women's World Cup is to be hosted by Poland next month.

English newspapers The Times, the Guardian and news agency Reuters reported on Wednesday that UEFA, football's European governing body, was set to drop its threat to boycott all FIFA tournaments.

The decision to allow European teams to participate in next month's Under-20 Women's World Cup in Poland came after UEFA had reportedly received guarantees that football's world governing body would not revive a plan to sell a stake in FIFA tournaments to private investors. FIFA President Gianni Infantino had dropped his plan to create a commercial subsidiary called FIFA Forward Enterprises (FFE) in the face of widespread protest last month.

UEFA spearheaded opposition to the plan but it had also demanded that "assurances have to be made that such attempts to disfigure the game in this way will never be made again," something that until now, FIFA had declined to do. The reports suggest this demand has now been met.

The reports also said UEFA would use a meeting of its executive committee and most of the presidents of its 55 national associations in Monaco on Thursday to inform them that the U20 tournament could go ahead.

'Not a UEFA defeat'

The Guardian reported that the FIFA and UEFA officials had been in private talks for weeks with the aim of preventing a boycott.

"It's not a UEFA defeat, rather the reality of avoiding hurting young players during a once in a lifetime ⁠opportunity," a source familiar with the discussions told Reuters. "The actions and insistence on change will ​continue."

The Times reported that UEFA was working on other ways to try to step up the pressure on Infantino.

It cited a letter reading that "UEFA hereby gives formal notice that it is actively considering legal action, arbitration, and/or regulatory complaints arising out of and in connection with the FFE plan proposed by FIFA and all related matters.

"You and FIFA are required to take immediate steps to identify, locate, and preserve all documents and electronically stored information described in this notice that are in your or FIFA's possession, custody, or control."

'Best possible conditions' for the tournament

Prior to the latest reports, the Polish FA (PZPN) told DW in a statement that it was continuing with preparations to host the Under-20 Women's World Cup as planned.

"Our priority remains to ensure the best possible conditions for the competition and for all participating teams," the statement read.

"For many of these young players, this tournament represents an important milestone in their sporting careers, and we remain fully focused on delivering an event worthy of their talent and commitment."

The tournament kicks off with the opening match between Poland and Argentina in Katowice on September 5.

Gianni Infantino is expected to stand for re-election at a FIFA Congress next March and so far no other candidate has come forward to challenge him. UEFA President Aleksander Ceferin has already said he will not run.

Edited by: Jonathan Harding

World.title: Could Syria become the focus of an Israeli-Turkish conflict?
World.content:
An Israeli attack on a Syrian military airfield just recently demonstrated once again that Syria is becoming a key battleground for the rivalry between regional powers. At the forefront: Israel and Turkey.

Following US mediation, Syrian and Israeli representatives met in Jordan last weekend for the first time in months. The talks aimed to defuse tensions following the recent Israeli attacks on Syrian territory and prevent hostilities between Israel and Turkey from spilling over into Syria.

The escalation was sparked by an Israeli attack on the Abu Duhur military airfield in Idlib Province on August 18. According to Syrian sources, the attack struck the runway and storage facilities without causing any fatalities. Israel stated that Syria had violated — or threatened to violate — a previous security agreement by allowing Turkish troops to use the airfield. Damascus and Ankara rejected these allegations.

The US criticized the attack by its Israeli ally as an "unnecessary escalation." In diplomatic terms, this amounts to a fairly clear show of rhetorical support for Ankara and Damascus.

Israel views a potential Turkish military presence in Syria as a red line. Yet, it remains unclear whether such a deployment is planned in the long term or whether it was even imminent at the time of the attack. Evidence on this matter is not publicly available.

However, as early as April 2025, Reuters news agency cited anonymous sources saying Turkey had inspected at least three air bases in Syria where it might want to station troops as part of a planned joint defense pact. Israeli airstrikes were already taking place at that time as well.

The Washington-based think tank Foundation for Defense of Democracies (FDD), which is considered pro-Israel, justifies the attack as follows : "Israel worries that Ankara could eventually use its military presence in Syria as a platform to pressure or threaten Israel, and remains wary of the close relationship between Syrian President Ahmad al-Sharaa and the Turkish leadership."

The Kurdish forces in Syria's northeast announced their dissolution on Tuesday, August 25, 2026 Image: Anagha Subhash Nair/Anadolu/picture alliance

Syria, Turkey and Israel disagree on the future order

For Bente Scheller, Syria expert at the German Green Party-affiliated Heinrich Böll Foundation, this explanation falls short.

"There is no evidence so far that Turkish troops are actually supposed to be stationed there," she told DW. While Israel may indeed have its own intelligence, the recent attack must be viewed against the backdrop of Israel's overall policy toward Syria as well as Turkey's growing regional role, she noted.

Marcus Schneider, a Middle East analyst at Germany's Friedrich Ebert Foundation — which is affiliated with the German Social Democratic Party (SPD) — in Beirut, also points out that a struggle for power and influence is unfolding in Syria and beyond.

"The attack primarily raises the question of what kind of military order will emerge in Syria in the future," he told DW. In his view, Israel wants to keep Syria weak, as a sovereign state that controls its own airspace would restrict Israel's military freedom of action. "The corridor for attacks against Iran runs through Syria," explained Schneider. A sovereign Syria could therefore pose a strategic obstacle to Israel.

Following the Hamas terror attacks on Israel on October 7, Israel's heightened security concerns are understandable, adds Scheller. In addition, Israel is certainly viewing with concern another development that extends beyond Syria.

"Israel is undoubtedly aware of how Turkey is currently attempting to position itself as a regional hegemon," Scheller said. The attack on Abu al-Duhur is therefore "clearly also a message to Turkey."

Turkey supports Syrian President al-Sharaa and is committed to a unified Syria which includes the territory in the country's northeast, where the majority of Syria's Kurdish population is located. For years, Turkey has been attacking the former Kurdish-led autonomous zone along its southern border. On Tuesday, the commander of the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces announced the official dissolution of the group.

An analysis by the US think tank Carnegie Foundation describes the situation as a strategic rivalry between Israel and Turkey: "The northeast is also the main arena where two externally-driven strategic visions for Syria collide." The International Crisis Group also views Syria as a fault line between Turkey, a rising regional power, and Israel.

The Uncertain Future of the Kurds in the new Syria To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Syria's closer relations with the US

Syria's improved relations with the US — which amount to US support — offer new prospects for the country, despite the Islamist past of its new leader, President Ahmad al-Sharaa. In summer 2025, the US began gradually easing sanctions, and in November of that year, al-Sharaa was received by US President Trump at the White House. The two met again on the sidelines of the NATO summit in Ankara in July 2026. In early 2026, the US withdrew its military forces from Syria, and on Monday (August 24), it officially removed the country from its list of state sponsors of terrorism.

However, under the current circumstances, Syria appears to be relying primarily on itself, including in its relations with Turkey. For analyst Marcus Schneider, however, a potential Turkish presence is not comparable to the former Iranian presence during the Assad regime.

Contrary to the view held in Israel, he argues that Ankara is primarily interested in a stable Syria and in securing its southern border. "The idea that Turkey, a NATO member, would attack Israel, a nuclear power, is preposterous," he said. The real problem, he argues, is that Israel increasingly views Turkey as a strategic adversary and interprets Turkey's capabilities as evidence of hostile intentions.

Al-Sharaa is seeking foreign policy support wherever he can find it, observes Scheller. "In recent months, Turkey has increasingly become one of the countries from which Damascus expects concrete assistance." This is not just a matter of security: Ankara wants to expand its regional influence and, at the same time, has an interest in maintaining stability along the shared border, she said.

US President Donald Trump is a strong supporter of Syrian President Ahmad al-Sharaa Image: Saul Loeb/AFP

Who will ultimately determine Syria's security order?

Following the overthrow of Syria's longtime ruler Bashar Assad in December 2024, Israel established a security zone north of the Golan Heights and has repeatedly attacked Syrian targets. According to an analysis by the Carnegie Foundation, the calls for such a buffer zone is deeply rooted in Israeli security thinking; less clear, however, is the intention — sometimes attributed to Israel by analysts — of permanently fragmenting Syria to keep it weak.

The US think tank FDD takes a different view, pointing to Israel's skepticism toward the new Syrian military and Turkish support. However, Schneider notes that the new regime in Syria has extended a hand to Israel from the outset, despite its ideological origins. "Damascus does not want a war with Israel," he said, adding that it wants to regain its national sovereignty. It is precisely this aspiration that clashes with Israel's military presence and its red lines.

Syria needs a viable political order

"Syria is caught between two militarily powerful neighbors that respect neither its sovereignty nor its territorial integrity," said Scheller.

In her view, the outcome will now depend on al-Sharaa's negotiating skills. "How can he defend Syrian sovereignty against these two neighbors and actually chart a distinct Syrian path?" However, Syria's weakness does not lie solely in its military inferiority. The country must first develop a viable political order, she notes.

This is also the starting point for political scientist Haid Haid in an analysis for the British think tank Chatham House: "Syria's foreign policy success has been significant, but it cannot, on its own, secure stability. In this sense, Syria's greatest vulnerability lies not at its borders, but within."

This article was originally published in German.

World.title: Zambia after the polls: A test for democracy in Africa
World.content:
Zambia's democratic institutions are under scrutiny, as the opposition continues to dispute the election results and courts remain closed. Weeks after the election, Zambia’s election story might be far from over.

The Electoral Commission of Zambia has declared incumbent President Hakainde Hichilema winner of the August 13 presidential election.

His closest challenger, Brian Mundubile, received 38% of the vote, according to official results published last week. However, Mundubile has since announced on several occasions that he would be challenging that result, and that his National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP) "shall not relent" in the face of any obstacle.

That challenge, however, comes as Zambia's courts have all remained closed since August 24 until further notice, with officials citing "security concerns."

The timing of this closure has raised questions about opposition voices having access to judicial election safeguards during this crucial stage of the post-election process, as random reports of irregularities continue to surface.

Opposition leader Brian Mundubile disputes the official election result despite its broad support by election monitors Image: Kathy Short/DW

Election dispute continues to unfold

The Law Association of Zambia (LAZ) has called for the urgent restoration of access to the courts and for alternative arrangements to be enacted for urgent cases.

LAZ President Arnold Kaluba said security measures must not undermine any access to justice or judicial independence.

"Such measures must be lawful, proportionate and implemented in a manner that preserves access to justice and respects the constitutional independence and autonomy of the judiciary," he stressed.

Meanwhile, the Human Rights Commission of Zambia has also expressed concern; its chairperson, Pamela Towela Sambo, warned that disruption to judicial operations could affect fundamental rights in the country, including access to a fair trial and legal remedies.

"[If] the right to a fair trial is delayed, there is increased risk of arbitrary detentions, while access to remedies is effectively blocked," she said.

Human rights defender Pamela Towela Sambo highlights that the ongoing closure of courts means that there is no access to due process Image: Human Rights Commission Media

'Irregular' submission of petition documents

However, the ongoing election dispute has taken a new turn: Zambia's Chief Justice Mumba Malila, acknowledged on August 25 that he had received documents described as a presidential election petition through his private email-address.

Malila described the method of submission as "highly irregular" —despite the current circumstances allowing no access to legal procedures. He said he nevertheless referred the documents to the Constitutional Court to determine whether this qualified as a petition having been formally filed.

The distinction here is important: The receipt of such documents does not confirm that a presidential election petition has been formally lodged per se.

The latest development comes as the courts remain closed, adding to questions about how election-related cases can be filed and processed.

Our time is now: Zambia's youth running in elections To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Government continues to cite security concerns for court closure

Meanwhile, the presidency has rejected suggestions that the court closures were intended to prevent and intervene with any challenges to the election result.

Hichilema's chief communications specialist Clayson Hamasaka said the security measures were of a "intelligence-led and preventive" nature, adding that they involved several government institutions beyond courts, and that they were intended to protect officials, institutions and members of the public.

He also maintained that people with legitimate grievances remained free to pursue remedies provided by law.

But during the election itself, there had already been suspensions of voting at some ballot boxes amid reports of violence. Questions about the independence of the media had also surface in the run-up to the vote.

President Hichilema appears to be pleased with his reelection — though some continue to claim that it wasn't fair and square Image: Anita Reed/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

Concerns about access to justice and public confidence remain strong, especially against this backdrop; the Zambia Executive Director Maurice Nyambe of Transparency International said in this context the country needs stronger institutions for resolving political disputes.

"At this stage of the electoral process, Zambia does not need fewer avenues for resolving political disputes. It needs stronger, accessible, and trusted institutions through which those disputes can be peacefully resolved."

Political commentator and human rights activist Laura Miti meanwhile questioned the lack of a fuller public explanation for the closure, writing on Facebook that "if you are going to unprecedentedly close the courts, you owe the nation an explanation beyond a blanket — there is a security threat."

A test beyond the ballot box

Zambia has long been regarded as one of Southern Africa's more stable multiparty democracies with a reputation for political stability and peaceful transfers of power.

But the current dispute comes at a time when democratic institutions across the region keep facing growing scrutiny over contested elections and political transitions. Therefore, the handling of situation will likely be observed beyond Zambia and the southern African region.

For Zambians, the issue goes beyond the contest between Hichilema and Mundubile; it is about how political disagreements can be resolved peacefully through independent, accessible and trusted institutions.

That notion is perhaps best reflected on the streets of Lusaka; a citizen of the capital simply told DW: "We are anxious and afraid because we do not know the truth about what is happening."

World.title: Moscow confirms visit of CIA Director John Ratcliffe
World.content:
The Russian government said that spy chief John Ratcliffe held talks with counterparts, but not President Vladimir Putin, on his Moscow trip.

The Kremlin confirmed on Wednesday that US foreign intelligence chief John Ratcliffe had held a series of high-level talks the previous day in Moscow, but denied reports that he had spoken with President Vladimir Putin.

CIA Director Ratcliffe had "contacts between security services," according to Russian government spokesman Dmitry Peskov.

Peskov said that President Putin had been "informed without delay" as to the content of the talks, but had not attended the meetings.

He added that he was unsure if the discussions could move US-Russian relations out of their current "profound crisis" and would not confirm if the group had discussed the Russian invasion of Ukraine.

Talks come as Iran truce stalls

Multiple US outlets reported on Ratcliffe's visit, but US President Donald Trump's administration has yet to comment on the trip. There were however photos of Ratcliffe's military plane landing in Latvia shortly before the meetings.

A military plane believed to be carrying Ratcliffe had landed near Riga, Latvia before he headed off to Moscow on another flight Image: @alfredspodins via X/REUTERS

The last time a CIA director visited Moscow was Ratcliffe's predecessor William Burns in November 2021. Russia launched its war against Ukraine three months later in February 2022.

Tuesday's talks came as truce negotiations between the US and Iran have stalled. Moscow had previously offered to act as a broker between the two parties over the conflict.

World.title: Gamescom 2026 highlights gaming industry's strength, AI challenges
World.content:
Gamescom 2026 opens in Cologne as the global gaming industry continues to grow. But rising hardware costs, AI concerns and slowing user growth all pose challenges.

Earlier this month, gaming giant Electronic Arts was sold to an investment consortium including Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund and US President Donald Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, for $55 billion (€47 billion).

The deal stood out in a few ways. It is believed to be one of the largest leveraged buyouts in history, meaning a significant chunk of the $55 billion was borrowed money that the company itself will have to pay back.

It was also the second-biggest deal in gaming history, after Microsoft's purchase of Activision Blizzard, the company behind the "Call of Duty" franchise, for $69 billion in 2023.

The Electronic Arts sale additionally shone a light on the growing economic significance of the gaming industry and the increasing interest from major global investors such as Saudi Arabia, seeking to benefit from the sector's cultural and financial clout.

Gamescom — a massive global gathering

That cultural and financial clout will be on full display over the next few days in the German city of Cologne, where Gamescom, the world's largest gaming event and trade fair, takes place.

The event attracts thousands of exhibitors and games developers, close to half a million visitors and many more millions of fans connecting online from around the world.

It's the place where companies build hype for their upcoming releases, with massive rooms packed with screens, consoles and a range of gaming experiences.

Robots impress at China's World Humanoid Robot Games To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"Gamescom is a very useful barometer for the health and mindset of the industry," Piers Harding-Rolls, a games industry analyst with Ampere, told DW.

That health looks fairly robust at present.

The global games market is currently valued at $213.9 billion, up 6.1% year on year, according to Newzoo, a gaming industry market analysis company. Manu Rosier, the company's director of market intelligence, says that growth is broad across the sector's three main platforms: mobile, console and PC.

It now comfortably rivals the movie and music businesses both in terms of finances and, some would argue, cultural significance and reach.

"If you add the music subscription and transactional markets together with the cinema box office, spending on games is over three times bigger," said Harding-Rolls.

Gamescom 2026 takes place from August 26-30 in Cologne, Germany, and could once again bring in close to half a million visitors Image: Wolf von Dewitz/dpa/picture alliance

Joost van Dreunen, an assistant professor at NYU Stern School of Business and the author of "One Up: Creativity, Competition, and the Global Business of Video Games," says gaming's communal aspects have powered its growth.

"The cultural relevance of interactive entertainment has substantially expanded in the past few years, as millions of players around the world have found a common interest in playing together online," he told DW. "That's something few other forms of entertainment have accomplished."

AI creates new challenges for gaming

Yet the sector faces significant challenges. Like most industries, it is grappling with artificial intelligence (AI) and an onslaught of AI-generated material.

"AI is flooding the existing digital markets with content that is generally disregarded by players," said van Dreunen. "It nevertheless makes it more difficult for audiences to find relevant content in an expanding sea of slop."

There is already clear evidence of resistance from gamers toward AI. A recent survey by Quantic Foundry, a gaming analytics company, found that 85% of respondents had a less than neutral position on generative AI.

Another challenge AI is bringing to the gaming industry is cost related. The development of AI infrastructure and data centers has led to a surge in demand for chips and memory, which has driven prices up. Nvidia recently warned some of its largest customers that semiconductor prices would increase by as much as 15%.

That has driven up component costs for the gaming sector. "It shows on every platform. PC builds and upgrades, console prices climbing mid-cycle rather than falling as they did in past generations, and rising smartphone prices," said Rosier.

He thinks the increased costs could delay the introduction of the next generation of games console in the next few years, while Piers Harding-Rolls thinks it is adding pressure to a sector grappling with other financial concerns.

"Increasing costs for games hardware components pushing up prices, hyper-competition across all areas of the market meaning a glut of content, and challenges in discovery (of new users) and user acquisition," he said.

Hooked on video gaming To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Joost van Dreunen also cautions that the sector is now more dominated by the biggest players than in previous years, with major releases this year such as the latest "Grand Theft Auto" and Marvel's "Wolverine" helping boost overall revenues.

"Demand is more top-heavy than in the boom years, which makes it really strong at the top and precarious in the middle," he said.

Another challenge is keeping gamers gaming and adding new ones. Manu Rosier says there are now 3.7 billion gamers around the world, more than 40% of the global population and more than 60% of all those who use the internet. However, there are signs that new user growth is slowing, he says.

Gaming enters a new phase of growth

Yet as the industry gathers in Cologne, there is an unmistakable optimism about its prospects. Beyond the gloom around AI, there is the belief that technology could also significantly reduce costs.

"AI is being used across games companies to replace repetitive tasks that are better done by agents including preproduction work and coding. This saves time and hopefully delivers efficiency, with the aim of cutting cost," said Harding-Rolls.

As for its ability to improve gameplay, many gamers remain doubtful. That's in part because the definition of a "gamer" has shifted, which has helped the industry itself evolve.

Popular titles such as 'Grand Theft Auto' and Marvel's 'Wolverine' are powering major growth for the industry in 2026 Image: Rockstar/dpa/picture alliance

"A generation ago, games were predominantly single-player focused and narrative-driven. Today, games are more social and less focused on story," said van Dreunen.

Yet that in turn brings its own challenge, with developers competing for the attention of billions of gamers around the world in a more crowded market.

"The market is continually evolving and reinventing itself," added Harding-Rolls. "Companies are continually challenged to innovate and bring new experiences to consumers."

Edited by: Tim Rooks

World.title: India: Assam tea industry faces climate-driven labor crisis
World.content:
Plantations in Assam produce more than half of India's tea. But rising heat is hurting yields, workers are increasingly leaving for more stable work, and producers are feeling the squeeze of stagnant tea prices.

The problems facing upper Assam's tea gardens are becoming increasingly difficult to ignore for workers like Bidesh Kamar and Sumitra Tanti.

Recent floods disrupted work for weeks in the northeast Indian state, adding even more uncertainty to their already precarious livelihood. More than 50 tea gardens were damaged following a devastating storm that swept across parts of Assam.

"Life has become unpredictable," Tanti told DW. "The weather can disrupt work, while wages remain low and work is not as dependable as it once was," she added.

Kamar said the economics of tea have changed.

"Tea is not as profitable as it once was, and there is less certainty about the work," Kamar told DW.

After 15 years working on tea plantations, Kamar is now considering whether it is time to "move on to greener pastures."

Assam's dwindling tea workforce

Their experience points to a growing problem for Assam's tea industry. With the business becoming less profitable and working conditions more uncertain, the industry is struggling to retain the experienced workforce which forms the backbone of the state's tea production.

Assam produces about 52% of India's tea and supports around 700,000 plantation workers and 140,000 small tea growers.

Hundreds of thousands of Assam residents rely on tea industry for work Image: Sahiba Chawdhary/REUTERS

For generations, its tea plantations have depended on a vast workforce picking leaves by hand.

But that model is now under pressure as the climate gets hotter, tea becomes less profitable and locals increasingly look elsewhere for work.

Oversupply has pushed prices down, while higher wages, fertilizer and fuel costs are squeezing producers.

Sanjiv Gogoi, who owns the 400-acre (162-hectare) Sanjiv Tea estate, said tea producers are grappling with a whole range of problems.

"Productivity has fallen, and the labor supply is not always reliable. More workers are leaving the plantations because the work no longer pays enough," Gogoi told DW.

The pressure is even greater on small growers, who produce nearly half of Assam's tea, he said.

"They have little bargaining power and often have to sell their freshly picked leaves to factories at low prices."

A changing landscape for tea

At the same time, erratic rainfall, rising temperatures and new pests are reducing yields and making traditional tea-growing areas increasingly vulnerable.

In Assam's major tea-growing districts, temperatures now regularly reach 36 to 40 degrees Celsius (97-104 degrees Fahrenheit), putting both tea plants and workers under severe heat stress.

Research shows that every 1°C rise in temperature can reduce tea yields by about 87 kilos per hectare in India.

For tea workers, who spend hours outdoors picking leaves, extreme heat adds another physical strain to already demanding work, with dehydration, exhaustion and fainting reported during the hottest hours.

Flooding poses an escalating threat to Assam's tea industry Image: Prabhakar Mani Tiwari/DW

Tea deflation drives workers away

According to statistics from India's North Eastern Tea Association (NETA), tea prices have barely kept pace with the rising cost of producing the crop. Moreover, labor costs now account for roughly 60% of all production costs, leaving plantations squeezed between rising wages and weak prices.

This has created a labor crisis. Plantation workers earn around 250 to 280 Indian Rupees (€2.30–€2.60 or $2.63-$2.94) a day, while unions are demanding 350 to 500 to reflect the rising cost of living.

"The most fundamental concern is the widening gap between the cost of producing tea and the price we realize from the market," Bidyananda Barkakoty, tea farmer adviser at NETA and former vice-chairman of the Tea Board of India, told DW.

He warned the departure of experienced workers was affecting both productivity and quality. Good tea depends on careful plucking of the right leaves, something that becomes harder when experienced workers are in short supply.

Meanwhile, absenteeism in some tea-growing districts has reportedly reached more than 50%, as workers choose construction, urban jobs or government employment schemes that offer better and faster returns.

New machines 'a necessity' for Assam's tea industry

Harkirat Singh Sidhu, a veteran tea planter with more than 55 years of experience across plantations in nine countries, says Assam's industry must adapt.

Climate change reshaping West Bengal's tea industry To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"We need to make the changes and not be pushed into making changes," Sidhu told DW.

He predicted that labor issues will only grow worse, "making mechanization a necessity rather than an option."

Sidhu advocates for regenerative farming to build resilient soil, combined with upgraded drainage networks, shade canopy management, and reduced reliance on chemical pesticides.

"Everything around us has changed, and so we need to seriously think out the changes we need to work out," he added.

As experienced workers leave the tea industry, estates increasingly rely on temporary or mechanical harvesting, which can further reduce quality and prices.

The result is a difficult downward spiral. Falling productivity reduces revenues, leaving estates with less money to invest in replanting, irrigation and measures to cope with the changing climate.

That, in turn, makes the industry even less attractive to workers.

"The younger generation will stay only when they see a future in the tea gardens, not merely a job," said Barkakoty.

That means better incomes and living conditions for workers, but also offering them skilled jobs through mechanization and technology.

World.title: Deadly flash flood wipes away villages in Nepal, Tibet
World.content:
Hundreds of people were reported missing, including 291 international tourists. Rescue helicopters have been unable to land in affected areas due to high floodwaters.

Several people were confirmed dead and hundreds more are missing after a flash flood swept through remote valleys in Nepal and Tibet on Wedensday.

The floodwaters washed away villages, damaged bridges and destroyed electrical infrastructure on both sides of the Nepal-China border.

"There is devastation everywhere we look," ‌Tula ​Bahadur BK, a health worker in Rasuwa district, told Reuters.

"The settlements next to the river have been completely swept away. Five of my own relatives are missing."

At 19 people were killed in Nepal while Chinese authorities also reported that a mudslide caused "major casualties" on the other side of the border in Tibet.

Security cameras captured the moment a wall of mud hit the Nepal-China border Image: REUTERS

Hundreds of people missing

Nepal's Tourism Board said 384 travelers were reported missing.

Among those missing travelers were including 291 foreign nationals, inculding 105 Indians.

A Nepali police spokesperson told Germany's DPA news agency that dozens of personnel were also missing.

"So far, we only have confirmation of 26 police personnel who remain missing in the flood," they said.

"We also have missing information of government revenue officials, hydropower workers among others. But we are still collecting the data."

Villages in Rasuwa district were swept away by the deluge of water and mud Image: Sunil Sharma/ZUMA/IMAGO

What caused the flash floods?

Nepal's Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal said an earthquake triggered an avalanche in the Himalayas that then triggered flash floods in the valleys below.

Chinese state news agency Xinhua said a mudslide on the Nepali side of the mountains spread to Gyirong County in Tibet.

The burst river also inundated villages in Dhading district Image: REUTERS

Major rescue operations underway

Nepal dispatched more than a dozen rescue helicopters to the mountainous Rasuwa region, but floodwaters were too high for the helicopters to land.

Nepali Prime Minister Balendra Shah said the military and police were assisting with rescues.

"Instructions have been given ... to move ​the people living in the lower areas ⁠to safer places," he said. "People along the river are advised to exercise extra caution and remain alert."

Chinese President Xi Jinping also ordered an "all out" rescue effort.

He said "the most urgent task is doing everything possible to search for and rescue the missing people... quickly treat injured people and minimize casualties to the greatest extent possible," according to Chinese state media.

Rescue helocopters were initually unable to land due to the high floodwaters Image: Prabin Ranabhat/AFP

A second flood may be imminent, according to Qianggong Zhang, head of climate and environmental risks at the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development.

"With a blockage still lodged upstream on the Nepal-China border river, authorities warn a second flood may occur," he told the AFP news agency.
